en: The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka:
"O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious;
O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious."
With steadfast limbs and bodies, praising [thee],
may we attain that life-span ordained by the gods; may Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being.
May Pūṣan and all the gods grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya with his unbroken wheel grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.

Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones. With firm limbs and bodies, offering praise, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods. May Indra, of far-reaching fame, grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. From every water, from every source—both from here and from there—may Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya together fashion prosperity through their wisdom.

The Vāyvaśvas, lords of the rays; the Marīcyātmanas, free from malice; the goddesses who give birth to the world—beget for me the state of having sons! The Mahānāmnīs, of great measure; the Mahasas, their own great splendors; the goddesses who give birth to Parjanya—beget for me the state of having sons! Drive away heat, drive away the Rākṣasa; drive away heat, drive away the Raghu; drive away the Ghra, drive away misfortune; drive them away, O goddesses, as you are impelled! The goddesses who have hurled the thunderbolt and the Ajītās; the goddesses who give birth to the world; the Ādityas and the goddess Aditi—[beget for me the state of having sons!]

May they rise upward from the womb. May the divine waters and plants be most auspicious for our welfare. O Sarasvatī, be gracious; may your expanse not be seen [by us]. From there, the two plants have been pressed out.

Memory, perception, tradition, and inference—this fourfold means shall establish the solar orb. The Sun draws up the moisture from the entire world; by the specific nature of its ripening, the distinctions of time are remembered. Just as a certain river flows inexhaustibly from its source, so do rivers flow toward it; though vast, that river does not turn back. In this same way, times arising from various origins are dependent upon the year.

Both minute and great, all join together in him; pervaded by them all, though vast, he does not turn back. One should know him as being above the year. That very same [sign] is in the *lakṣaṇa* (mark): mounted upon both the minute and the great, he is clearly seen. The year is not clearly seen as a distinct being (*nādhisattva*). "Scaly, moist, and tawny"—this is the mark of Varuṇa. Wherever this is clearly seen, there a thousand [cows] are led.

For there is one head with various faces; that is the entirety characterized by the seasons. On both sides are seven sense organs. Indeed, what is spoken is smeared [upon it]. The white and the black belong to the year, on its right and left flanks. Regarding this, there is this verse: "One part of you is bright, another part is worshipful; you are like the sky, possessing two days of different forms. For you, O self-dependent one, protect all wondrous powers. May your gift here, O Pūṣan, be auspicious. Herein there is no world, no Pūṣan, and no cattle.

The sun is not [the most beloved]; rather, one should know that the year itself is most beloved through direct perception. This indeed is the most beloved form of the year: when some great misfortune is about to befall him, [the teacher says], "Perform this meritorious act! To him, he should give the means for its accomplishment—just as the characteristic of the seasons is the world and the seven [sages].

Of those born together, they say the seventh is the one born alone; the six are the striving seers, born of the gods. Their desired abodes have been established according to their stations; they tremble for the Sustainer, transformed according to their forms. Who indeed, O mortals, being unprovoked, has spoken thus to his friend: "Who among us seeks to abandon us"? He who has abandoned a friend who knows him—of him there is no enjoyment even in speech. Even if he hears, he hears in vain; for he does not know the path of righteous action. Being impelled by season after season...

The "Vinanādābhidhāva" [is the name of a ritual]; there are sixty and thirty *valgā* [reins or divisions]; and the two, Śukla and Kṛṣṇa, are the sixty-fold ones. Jaradakṣa is with garments of deep red; Vasanta is with the Vasus. Of the year, of Savitṛ, he is remembered as the first performer of the *praiṣa* (directions). "Strike those others," and "protect these"—these words are employed where this is observed. One should understand it to be exactly this: the authority regarding the succession of time. However, we shall state the specific distinctions.

Learn now concerning the seasons. The host of Rudras, clad in white garments, returns together with the summer; he strikes down the entire earth with an incomparable light. Learn now concerning the Ādityas: they bestow the fruit of the year-long ritual through the rains. Free from suffering, yet appearing as if possessed by the eye of suffering, he is seen as if yellowed by bile. Not causing distress through cold, he appears as if weeping with red eyes; he gladdens and indeed blazes forth.
And his two eyes become calm. Indeed, those offspring that fall away do so after a year; those that remain established remain established after a year—meaning, after the rains.
He hears others, indeed all six.

It is for one who has arisen from the pain of the eyes; the pupils are perfectly clear. There is no ointment for the eye. Learn that of the Ṛbhus: garments with the luster of gold; learn that they are unwashed (new). "Eat food, cleanse yourselves; I am the giver of life to you"—these are the words employed. Wherever it is seen in autumn, the hosts of Maruts, possessing wind, appear as if shaking and striking, like the tip of an arrow aimed from yonder to conquer. They are seen together, fully armed.

[They are] like discarded skins of animals; [they are] the matted locks of Śiva; [the eyes of one] about to fight who is not yet angry; [the eyes of one] who is angry are as red; one should know the two eyes of gold; [they are] like those of a bowman; there is famine even among the gods; water is in the house of men; these words speaking aloud; the lightning-flashes of the cold season pass away; Agni Pavamāna beheld them; seeing no means of livelihood here; for him this [verse] occurs: "Here, here, O Maruts, you of pure austerity, sun-skinned, I choose your wide-spreading shelter; I choose it as if it were visible."

The garments are deep red; the *aṣṭivajrī* and the *śataghnī*—the All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*) carry them away, they who are wise and whose tongue is fire, never failing. Neither god nor mortal, neither King Varuṇa the pervasive, nor Agni, nor Indra, nor Pavamāna knows its mother. One end of the divine bow rests in heaven, the other is fixed upon the earth. Indra himself, in the form of an ant, cut the bowstring of that bow. That bow of Indra is called "the unanointed" (*ajyam*); they speak of it among those of cloud-like color.

This very [rite] belongs to Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya; this is the bow of Rudra. Indeed, it was the tip of the string of Rudra’s bow that crushed his head. That became the Pravargya. Therefore, he who sacrifices with a sacrifice accompanied by the Pravargya restores the head of Rudra; Rudra does not seek to harm him who knows thus. He sacrifices having rested [the fires], and three...

With eyes turned far upward and looking askance, Śiśira appears; neither his form nor his garments can be seen, nor is his eye visible. Yet he does not harm one another; that indeed is the characteristic mark of a god. With red eyes and a variegated head, facing toward the rising sun, you make the *nyañjalikā* gesture; you make the *nijānukā* gesture. "The *nijānukā* is mine, the *nyañjalikā* is yours; let these wait upon my word. To him, all the seasons bow down.

Because he establishes the boundary, the Brāhmaṇa attains the office of Purohita—he who knows thus. Indeed, that year, together with these generals (*senānī*), brings all desires to Indra. He is the drop (*drapsa*). Regarding him, there is this verse: "The drop descended upon the *Aṃśumatī*, moving along, black, with ten thousand [followers]. Indra, by his power, [overcame] him as he was blowing [the fire] in the whirlpool; O you of heroic mind, blow upon him and then run away! By means of this very [verse], Indra [acted] together with the Salāvṛkī.

He looks down upon the Asuras. The earth is radiant; the year and the sky are established upon her. A teacher and a pupil who know this should not bear malice toward one another. He who bears malice falls from the heavenly world. Thus end the sections on the circles of the seasons (*ṛtumaṇḍala*). These are narratives concerning the circles of the sun (*sūryamaṇḍala*); hereafter follow those with etymological explanations (*sanirvacana*). "They should bear malice toward their own kin"—thus [ends the section]. And five [verses], according to Sāyaṇa’s commentary: Āroga, Bhrāja, Paṭara, Pataṅga.

"The golden one, possessing light, is radiant; they all heat the sky for him, milking out vigor, not failing. Kaśyapa is the eighth. He does not leave Mahāmeru. Regarding him, there is this verse: "O Kaśyapa, that craft of yours which is luminous, powerful, abundant, and of wondrous brilliance, in which the seven suns are placed together—to that birthplace may I resort. All of them receive light from Kaśyapa for his sake.

"Soma expels them from Kaśyapa, just as one who has failed in his work [is expelled]. "The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are the life-force of the senses; there are seven vital breaths in the head," say the teachers, "the Sūryas. "I have seen these seven Sūryas," said Pañcakarṇa Vātsyāyana and Saptakarṇa Plākṣi. "Kaśyapa is our traditional authority (*ānuśravika*)," they both declare. "Indeed, we were unable to go to Mount Mahāmeru."

"I saw this solar orb revolving," said Gārgya. "It goes toward the Great Meru, yet it leaves one [spot] behind. "The *bhrāja*, *paṭara*, and *pataṅga* [rays] burn here; they stand and scorch. Therefore, here on earth there are those who are scorched by three heats, while the others are so in yonder world. Thus, here on earth there are those scorched by three heats. Regarding them, there is this verse: "Seven suns have entered into heaven; the giver of sacrificial fees follows them along their paths. They all scorch clarified butter for him."

"Yielding strength, not shrinking back"—thus [it is said]. "The seven officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the suns," say the teachers; regarding them, this verse occurs: "Seven directions with various suns, seven hotṛ-priests as officiants—the divine Ādityas who are seven—with them, O Soma, protect us. This is also the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "The one shining in the quarters creates the seasons. Vaiśampāyana says that by this very process, it extends up to the state of having a thousand suns. Regarding this, there is this verse:

"O Indra, if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths for you, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, even a thousand suns would not equal your birth; nor would the two worlds," so it is said. Because the seasons possess different characteristics, there is a multiplicity of suns. "But eight are determined," so it is said. There are eight solar orbs above that. Regarding them, this verse occurs: "The wondrous face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni. It has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-region."
"The Sun is the soul of that which moves and that which stands"—thus [says the scripture]. Sākapūṇi, Plākṣi, and Tapatritapa say there are various suns, nine suns in total.
Thus ends the seventh Anuvāka in the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Where does this cloud settle? Where is this year in relation to itself? Where, O God, are this day and this night? Where are the months and the seasons situated? The half-months and the moments (muhūrtas), along with the twinklings of the eye and the truṭis—where do these waters settle when they go forth from here at present? "The times (kālāḥ) settle in the waters; the waters are contained within the sun. The clouds enter into the waters; the lightning is contained within the sun. "These two earths are without color."

"This one and that one are the two worlds (rodasī). What, then, has been placed between them, by which these two are held apart? The two earths are held apart by Viṣṇu"—this is the Vatsa’s knowledge. "For you have become rich in food and rich in cows; you provide good pasture for man who desires to give. "Viṣṇu has propped apart these two worlds; you have supported the earth on all sides with your rays. What do they call the strength of that Viṣṇu? What is his splendor? What is his ultimate resort? That the God alone has sustained [all].

"He purifies both worlds, heaven and earth. They say that from Vāyu comes the strength of Viṣṇu; from the Imperishable (akṣara), radiance is said to arise. "The God supported [the world] with three feet; that which is the one supreme foot of Viṣṇu... "The fires and the winds indeed—this is his ultimate resort. "I ask you about the supreme death, the lowest, and the middle, and the world of merit and sin; this I ask you now. "They call that [Vāyu] the supreme death; Pavamāna is the middle; Agni alone is the lowest death."

"The moon is said to be the fourth," it is said. "Those without exertion go to supreme death; the wicked always go [there], while those with exertion go indeed to where the meritorious people dwell. Then they enter the middle [realm] and reach the four fires. "I ask you about the doers of evil, where Yama torments them; O Brahmin, tell us that, if you know the houses of the non-existent. The suns risen from Kaśyapa always strike down the wicked.

"In the intermediate spaces between heaven and earth, they are deposited there by the Vasus; thus they become bodiless, like the fruit of unmeritorious action—without hands, feet, or hair. There those people are not born from a womb; having died, they undergo death again, being devoured by their own deeds like *āśātika* worms. Then they are purified by the Vasus; he who knows this transcends death. Such indeed is the Brāhmaṇa who possesses this knowledge.

He is the one of supreme long hearing (*dīrghaśruttama*). He is Kaśyapa’s guest, the one whose going is perfected and whose coming is perfected. Regarding him, there is this verse: "In whom the seven Vasus grow—holy growths; he is indeed the seer of supreme long hearing, the heated offering (*gharma*) of Indra, the guest. Kaśyapa is the beholder, because he beholds everything due to his subtlety.

Now follows [the hymn] of Agni Aṣṭapuruṣa. Regarding him, there is this verse: "O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knowest all ways. Keep away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer to thee the most abundant word of homage. Thus it is said: "The one who is concentrated in mind is praised as the best; he is the ancient one who rises within his own abodes through his own deeds. Thus ends the eighth Anuvāka of the first Prapāṭhaka in the Kṛṣṇayajurvedīya Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.

"Agni and Jātavedas; Sahojas, Ajira, and Prabhu; Vaiśvānara and Naryāpas; Paṅktirādhas as the seventh; and Visarpi as the eighth among the Agnis—these are the eight Vasus who dwell on earth. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the specific colors of Agni's flames according to the seasons are mentioned: "the blue-flamed and the yellow-flamed," and so forth. Then there is Vāyu, who has eleven males and eleven females. They are radiant and pure; those belonging to Vāsuki and the lightning are silver-colored, harsh, and dark.

"The Kapilas, the very red ones, those moving upward and those falling downward, and the lightning—these are the eleven. One who knows this, the lightning does not strike. Vyāsa Pārāśarya said: "I desired death by lightning itself. [The text continues: "But it does not strike one who is unwilling, for he who knows thus. Then there are the hosts of Gandharvas: Svānabhrāj, Aṅghāri, Bambhāri, Hasta, Suhasta, Kṛśānu, and Viśvāvasu.

"Mūrdhanvān, Asūryavarcas, and Kṛti—these are the eleven classes of Gandharvas. "The gods and the Mahādevas; the gods Raśmis and Garagiras"—"poison does not harm him who knows this. "Gaurī has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, nine-footed, having become thousand-syllabled in the highest heaven. This is an epithet of Vāc (Speech). Now follow those [mantras] which are explained by their very utterance (*nigada*).

We shall enumerate them: the Varāhavahs, the Svatapases, the Vidyunmahas, the Dhūpayas, the Śvāpayas, and the Gṛhamedhas—these are they; as well as these Aśimidviṣas. These Parjanyas rain upon the earth with showers. They are the same [deities], though with reversed case-endings. Impelled by the seven winds, they rain upon those worlds. Of them, this verse occurs: "This water is the same, rising up and falling down through the days."

"The rain-clouds quicken the earth; the fires quicken the heavens. "That imperishable syllable, created by the beings, which all the gods worship—the Great Seer, they made Jamadagni its guardian. "Jamadagni is nourished by the meters increasing by four syllables each; we, satiated by King Soma and by the heroic Brahman, [declare]: 'Auspicious be the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions for us! "Therefore, we choose that peace and well-being, the path for the sacrifice, the path for the lord of the sacrifice."

"May there be divine well-being for us; may there be well-being from humans. May the healing medicine ascend upward. May there be peace for our bipeds; may there be peace for our quadrupeds. "O Soma-drinkers! O non-Soma-drinkers!"—these are explained by the *nigada* (recitation). "The pure ones slay the poison-eaters; those who have performed penance, being satisfied with water, [protect] the quadrupeds and the one."
Thus ends the ninth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"This earth has a thousandfold covering; the supreme sky has a thousandfold covering. O Aśvins, Nāsatyas, you who are the lords of the entire world. "The wife is the earth, the husband is the sky; as a couple, you two have overcome [the obstacles]. Bṛhaspati and Rudra are the sons; Saramā is the female and [her mate] the male. "One of you wears the bright [garment], the other wears the sacrificial [garment]; you two are like the two days of different forms, like the sky. For you two, possessing self-power (*svadhā*), protect all wondrous powers (*māyā*). O Pūṣans, may your gift here be auspicious."

"O Aśvins, the two wonderful ones, the repositories of the world, you who move together as companions across heaven and earth—O Aśvins, lords of splendor, come to my call with your donkey-drawn chariot, together with Sūryā. "O Aśvins, when Bhujyu was in the midst of the cloud, no one could carry him away, for he was like a stone. You carried him out on self-propelled ships that glide through the mid-air and are free from water. "O Nāsatyas, with winged steeds that traverse three nights and three days, you carried Bhujyu away."

"On the far shore of the ocean, of the dry land, and of the moist," [he says]. "With three chariots, hundred-footed and drawn by six horses"—thus [he speaks]. He binds Savitṛ as he extends himself; Śambara follows after him, as does Āpapūruṣamvara. "Savitṛ becomes stainless," [it is said]. Having recognized him as well-satisfied, the self-controlled Tugra follows him who utters many songs of Soma, through his crooked course, among those who are greedy for Soma. That battle is risen, risen, and risen further; he drinks the cows of speech.

"Praised with those cows, he passes beyond others and those who are not accompanied by *rakṣas*. He follows by turning around; thus, "O you two Aśvins, you are such. These two are heaven and earth. "Day after day you conceive the embryo," it is said. Of these two, these are the two calves: day and night. Day belongs to the earth; night belongs to heaven. When they are not released, they become husband and wife. Of these two, these are the two calves: Agni and Āditya. Night’s calf is the white Āditya; day’s calf is Agni.

The copper-colored one is Aruṇa; these two are not released. They become husband and wife. Of these two, these are the two calves: Vṛtra and Vaidyuta. Vṛtra belongs to Agni; Vaidyuta belongs to Āditya. These two are not released. They become husband and wife. Of these two, these are the two calves: Uṣman (heat) and Nīhāra (mist). Uṣman belongs to Vṛtra; Nīhāra belongs to Vaidyuta. Those two attain those very two. This Night, pregnant, dwells with her son. This indeed is her caul.

"Whatever rays there are at night; as the membrane (*ulbaṇa*) of a pregnant cow, so is this [membrane] of her. He becomes possessed of offspring and cattle who knows thus: "This one rising and setting," "The Sun is the calf of merit," and "Now the Pavitra-Aṅgirasas. You two are the masters of the waters, you maintain Agni; of those two, these two are the calves. (Four and four.)
Thus ends the tenth Anuvāka in the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Those possessing the *pavitra* sit around the prize (*vāja*). Their ancient father protects their vow. Varuṇa has hidden the great ocean; only the wise were able to grasp it within its foundations. "The *pavitra* is spread out for you, O Brahmaṇaspati. As the Lord, you encompass its limbs on every side. One whose body is not heated [by austerity] does not partake of that while raw; only those who are cooked [purified], carrying it, have attained it. "Brahmā is the lord of the gods... "They fashioned it from non-existence at once—the seven seers and Atri."

"All the three [worlds] and Agastya dwelt with the constellations, performing auspicious rites. Then, [the hymn] of Savitṛ Śyāvāśva Āvartikāma: "Those stars which are set on high, they are seen by night; where do they go by day? Unfailing are the ordinances of Varuṇa; the moon, the constellation, moves on, looking out. "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ, the divine, we meditate upon; may he impel our thoughts. "That of Savitṛ we choose."

"We are the food of the god, the most excellent, the best of all things. We long for the swift favor of Bhaga. Thus [they spoke]. Savitar concealed the three [worlds] from all the light of heaven; at night they became invisible to sight. "We shall be joined with bone to bone," they said. "My name is indeed Name; I am both neuter and male. I am stationary and I am moving. I have sacrificed, I sacrifice, and I shall sacrifice. By me the beings sacrificed; the beings are my cattle.

"I am the pervasive one who is to be followed. [He said: "Women indeed exist; they call them 'men' to me. "One with eyes sees, but the blind does not perceive; the son who is a seer (kavi) knows these things. "He who truly understands those [things] is the father of Savitṛ. "The blind man found a jewel; the fingerless man strung it on a thread; the neckless man put it on; the tongueless man praised it. "He who knows in truth the tree whose roots are above and whose branches are below—that person would never place his trust [in such a thing]."

"May Death not kill me"—thus [he spoke]. Laughter, weeping, and song; the lute, the drum, and the dance; the dead and the living—whatever it may be, know that to be his limbs, as it were. Not thirsting, he meditated while thirsting: "From this one born to me, moving in pairs, the son of Nirṛti was born, O Vaideha—the one who is both mindless and conscious. He found that jewel; he, though fingerless, strung it; he, though neckless, fastened it; he, though tongueless, tasted it.

"One should not enter the city after having known this Ṛṣi. If one should enter, one should enter after wandering about in secret. This is the vow for that origin. "O Agni, mount upon that chariot: single-horsed, of a single yoke; single-wheeled, with a single pole; whose course is as swift as the wind, O All-pervading One! "It does not suffer damage, it does not waver; its axle does not become stuck when it moves. When he mounts the chariot, having yoked to it white and red horses of Agni," "with one and with ten, O Self-existent One!"

"With two for our desire, and with twenty; with three and with thirty, O Vāyu, release those teams here. Thus they fashioned it; I have perceived my name; the song has been heard; it is released; it trembles—seven times.
Thus ends the eleventh anuvāka of the first prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 11 ||

"Spread out! Extend! Blow up! Blow down! Blow together! [Bestow] the forms of the moon upon the sun; place the embryo therein, he who is the man. Thus, what is poured from here goes to the sun. "Make the essence for the moon; generate fire from the waters at the beginning; he who alone is called Rudra. "Incalculable are the thousands; they are remembered but are not seen. Understand this thus. "Come, O Indra, with your pleasant bay horses, whose hair is like peacock feathers."

"Let no one, not even those with snares, restrain you; go as if toward a flowing stream. "O Indra, do not come with the pleasant bay horses whose hair is like peacock feathers; let no one, not even those with snares, restrain me; I go as if toward a flowing stream. "With small and large, with swift and unyoked steeds, with dark ones that have attained the color of green—O Indra, come harnessed with a thousand! "Agni is clothed in shimmering garments; Vāyu has white *sikatuka* [horses]; the Year [comes] with horses of various colors."

"Your attendants are eternal," thus [it is said]. "Subrahmaṇyom! Subrahmaṇyom! O Indra, come! O you with bay horses, come! From Medhātithi; from Meṣa; from Vṛṣaṇaśva; O Menā; O you who leap over the cow; O paramour of Ahalyā; O Kauśika Brahmin, you who call yourself Gautama! Thus [it is said]. "The ruddy-horsed ones have come here; the Vasus dwelling on earth; the eight Agnis clothed in the quarters; and these, namely Agni and Jātavedas. Thus [it is said]. "The copper-horsed ones, with copper chariots; copper-colored and likewise dark."

"Those with staffs in hand are eating and chewing; from here the Rudras have gone to the highest state. Thus was their place and measure described previously. "Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ have come here in all their forms by means of a water-path chariot; they are the 'water-drinkers' (apsuṣas) of the two," thus it is said. Their attire and garments have been described. From here follows the worship of the divisions of time. "The Vāsātyas" refers to the Aśvins. "Who is making a sound in the atmosphere?"—thus the descendant of Vasiṣṭha, Rauhiṇa, performed an inquiry.

Regarding this, there is this [verse]: "Like a thundering flash of lightning... and "Thou art the rising of Brahman; thou art the upward-rising of Brahman; thou art the spreading of Brahman; thou art the under-spreading of Brahman. And it is seen: "The two have gone to the further shore; six [spokes] were in the wheel."
Thus ends the twelfth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 12 ||

"I know this earth, which has eight wombs, eight sons, and eight wives; death is not mine, nor has immortality carried me away. "I know this intermediate space, which has eight wombs, eight sons, and eight feet; death is not mine, nor has immortality carried me away. "I know that sky, which has eight wombs, eight sons, and eight wives; death is not mine, nor has immortality carried me away. "The great, well-protecting earth... (and so forth).

"Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space; Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son; all the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi; Aditi is what has been born, Aditi is what is to be born. "Eight sons of Aditi were born from her body; with seven she approached the gods, but she cast Mārtāṇḍa away. "With seven sons, Aditi approached the former age; that was for the sake of progeny and death; thus she cast Mārtāṇḍa away."

We shall enumerate them: Mitra and Varuṇa; Dhātṛ and Aryaman; Aṃśa and Bhaga; Indra and Vivasvat—these [are they]. "Hiraṇyagarbha," "Haṃsa," "Śuciṣat," "Brahmajajñānam," and "Taditpadam"—these [are they]. The "Garbha" belongs to Prajāpati. Then there is the "Puruṣa" and the "Saptapuruṣa. With these seven, that heaven makes four.
Thus ends the thirteenth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 13 ||

"That sun which rises taking away the life-breaths (*prāṇa*) of all beings, may it not rise taking away the life-breaths of my offspring, nor those of my cattle, nor mine. That sun which sets taking away the life-breaths of all beings, may it not set taking away the life-breaths of my offspring, nor those of my cattle, nor mine. That sun which fills [the sky] filling itself with the life-breaths of all beings, may it not [fill] the life-breaths of my offspring, nor those of my cattle... [nor mine].

"May you not diminish me by my vital breaths," he says; for that which wanes diminishes by the vital breaths of all beings. "Not by my offspring, not by my cattle; may you not diminish me by my vital breaths," he says. These are the stars; they glide forth and glide back by the vital breaths of all beings. "Not by my offspring, not by my cattle; do not glide forth nor glide back from me by my vital breaths," he says. These are the months and the half-months.

"By means of the vital breaths of all beings, they glide away and glide upward. Let them not glide away from my offspring, nor from my cattle; let them not glide away from my vital breaths, nor glide upward! These seasons—by means of the vital breaths of all beings, they glide away and glide upward. Let them not glide away from my offspring, nor from my cattle; let them not glide away from my vital breaths, nor glide upward! This year—by means of the vital breaths of all beings, it glides away and glides upward."

"Do not creep away, do not crawl away, from my offspring, nor from my cattle, nor from my vital breaths. This day creeps away and crawls away from the vital breaths of all beings; [may it not do so] from my offspring, nor from my cattle, nor from my vital breaths. "This night creeps away and crawls away from the vital breaths of all beings; may it not creep away, may it not crawl away, from my offspring, nor from my cattle, nor from my vital breaths."

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. "This is your union; do not neglect our union. He fills [the vessels] with the vital breaths. "Do not creep away, and as it creeps forth, do not creep away—two and two. It rises and sets, it fills and wanes. These are the stars; these are the months; these are the seasons; this is the year; this is the day; this is the night; ten.
Thus ends the fourteenth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now, regarding the eightfold Āditya: "May I shine by my own splendor in the station of the Vasu Ādityas"; "May I shine by my own splendor in the station of the Rudra Ādityas"; "May I shine by my own splendor in the station of the True Ādityas"; "May I shine by my own splendor in the station of the Ādityas who blow forth and strike down"; "May I shine by my own splendor in the station of the Wind-like Maruts Ādityas"; "May I shine by my own splendor in the station of the Ṛbhu Ādityas"; [and] "Of the Year, of Savitṛ."

"May I shine by my own splendor in the place of Āditya. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. "O rays, you are my mate; do not disregard my mate. May I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Ṛbhus and the Ādityas—this is the sixth.
Thus ends the fifteenth anuvāka of the first prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

May I shine with my own splendor in the place of Āroga; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Bhrāja; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Paṭara; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Pataṅga; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Svarṇara; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Jyotiṣīmanta; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Vibhāsa; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Kaśyapa. Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ.
"O Waters, you are our mate; do not spurn our mating. Thus ends the ten [verses] of Āroga.
Thus ends the sixteenth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.16.

Or else, [I am] of Vāyu, who has eleven male consorts and eleven female consorts. I shine with my own splendor in the station of the radiant Rudras; I shine with my own splendor in the station of the white Rudras; I shine with my own splendor in the station of the Vāsuki-lightning Rudras; I shine with my own splendor in the station of the silver-colored Rudras; I shine with my own splendor in the station of the coarse Rudras; I shine with my own splendor in the station of the dark-hued Rudras.

I shine by my own splendor in the place of the tawny Rudras; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the deep-red Rudras; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the upward-moving Rudras; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the descending Rudras; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the lightning-like Rudras; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the radiant Rudrāṇīs; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the pure-white Rudrāṇīs.

I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Vāsukī and Vaidyutī Rudrāṇīs; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Rajatā Rudrāṇīs; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Paruṣā Rudrāṇīs; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Śyāmā Rudrāṇīs; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Kapilā Rudrāṇīs; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Atilohitī Rudrāṇīs; I shine by my own splendor in the place of the Ūrdhvā Rudrāṇīs.

May I shine by my own splendor in the place of the descending Rudrāṇīs; may I shine by my own splendor in the place of the lightning-like Rudrāṇīs. Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! O forms, you are a pair; do not disregard our union. May I shine by my own splendor in the place of the upward-moving Rudras; may I shine by my own splendor in the place of the deep-red Rudrāṇīs—five times.
Thus ends the seventeenth Anuvāka in the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.17.

Now, regarding the eightfold Agni: may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Agni of the eastern direction; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Jātavedas of the intermediate direction (southeast); may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Sahojas of the southern direction; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Ajirāprabhava of the intermediate direction (southwest); may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Vaiśvānara of the western direction; may I shine with my own splendor in the place of Naryāpas of the intermediate direction (northwest).

"May I shine by my own splendor in the place of Paṅtirādhas Udakdiśya; may I shine by my own splendor in the place of Visarpi Upadiśya. Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! O quarters, you are my mate; do not despise our union. And [he recites] "Svaraikaṃ ca."
These are the rays, the waters, the forms, and the five directions.
Thus ends the eighteenth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"In the south-eastern direction is the Visarpin hell; protect us from it! "In the south-western direction is the Avisarpin hell; protect us from it! "In the north-eastern direction is the Viṣādin hell; protect us from it! "In the north-western direction is the Aviṣādin hell; protect us from it! "In whom [reside] the seven Vasus and the senses, O Śatakratu!"—these [are the mantras]. There are nine [mantras] for the south-eastern direction.
Thus ends the nineteenth anuvāka of the first prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.19.

"May Indraghoṣa with the Vasus place you in the east; may Manojavasa with the Pitṛs place you in the south; may Pracetas with the Rudras place you in the west; may Viśvakarman with the Ādityas place you in the north; may Tvaṣṭṛ with the forms (rūpas) place you above; may Saṃjñāna [place you] behind. Thus it is said. "The Āditya is the entire fire on earth; Vāyu is in the intermediate space; Sūrya is in heaven; Candramas is in the quarters; the Nakṣatras are in their own world. Thus it is said.
"Thus indeed! Thus indeed, O Agni! Thus indeed, O Vāyu! Thus indeed, O Indra! Thus indeed, O Pūṣan! Thus indeed, O Gods!"—thus [he recites] in the directions; and there are seven [verses].
Thus ends the twentieth Anuvāka in the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.20.

All the waters, water after water—from this one, from that one, from here, from there—Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya have fashioned them together with wisdom. With Vāyu as their steed, the rays as their lords, having light as their essence, free from malice, these divine mothers who give birth to the world: for the sake of my possession of sons, O pressed juices, flow forth! You who are named Great, of great measure, mighty, more than mighty, celestial, divine, and born of Parjanya: for the sake of my possession of sons, O pressed juices, flow forth! Away with heat, away with the Rākṣasa; away with fever, away with sin; away with stench, and away with misfortune!

The gods have placed the divine, well-aimed thunderbolt; the divine ones have impelled the rays of light. The world is the progenitor of the gods; the Ādityas and the goddess Aditi—look upward from your source! O gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O worshipful ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain the lifespan ordained by the gods. May Indra, of far-reaching fame, grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being.

May Bṛhaspati grant us well-being. May the ruddy banners [of light] and the sages girt by the wind be our support, for they are established in a hundred ways and possess a thousandfold nourishment. May the divine waters and the plants be auspicious and most propitious to us; O Sarasvatī, be gracious to us, and may your vast expanse not appear before our eyes. Thus ends the twenty-first Anuvāka of the first Prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. (1.21)

"He who knows the flower of the waters becomes possessed of flowers, possessed of offspring, and possessed of cattle. The moon, indeed, is the flower of the waters. He who knows thus becomes possessed of flowers, possessed of offspring, and possessed of cattle. "He who knows the abode of the waters becomes possessed of an abode. Fire, indeed, is the abode of the waters. He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode. "He who knows the abode of fire becomes possessed of an abode. Water, indeed, is the abode of fire. He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode. "He who knows the abode of the waters..."

"He becomes possessed of a home. Wind, indeed, is the home of the waters; he who knows the home of wind becomes possessed of a home. He becomes possessed of a home—he who knows thus. Water, indeed, is the home of wind; he who knows thus becomes possessed of a home. He who knows the home of the waters becomes possessed of a home. Yonder sun, shining, is indeed the home of the waters; he who knows the home of yonder shining sun becomes possessed of a home. Water, indeed, is the home of yonder shining sun."

"He becomes possessed of a home who knows thus. He who knows the abode of the waters becomes possessed of a home. The moon, indeed, is the abode of the waters; he becomes possessed of a home who knows the abode of the moon. He becomes possessed of a home [who knows the abode] of the waters. Water, indeed, is the abode of the moon; he becomes possessed of a home who knows thus. He who knows the abode of the waters becomes possessed of a home. The stars, indeed, are the abode of the waters; he becomes possessed of a home.

"He who knows the abode of the stars becomes possessed of an abode. Water, indeed, is the abode of the stars; he who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode. "He who knows the abode of water becomes possessed of an abode. Parjanya (the rain-god), indeed, is the abode of water; he who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode. "He who knows the abode of Parjanya becomes possessed of an abode. Water, indeed, is the abode of Parjanya; he who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode. Thus it is said.

"He who knows the abode of the waters becomes possessed of an abode. The year, indeed, is the abode of the waters; he who knows the abode of the year becomes possessed of an abode. Water, indeed, is the abode of the year; he who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode. "He who knows the ship established upon the waters stands firm. These worlds, indeed, are established upon the waters. Regarding this, there is this verse:"

"Taking up the essence of the waters, the rising [light], the pure [substance] collected in the sun—that which is the essence of the essence of the waters, that most excellent one I take for you. These worlds are indeed the essence of the waters; they are collected in yonder sun. Having dug a northern altar (*uttaravedī*) knee-deep, having filled it with water up to the ankles, and having strewn it with lotus leaves, lotus stalks, and lotuses, one should carry the fire into that open space and kindle it.

The exponents of Brahman say: "Why is this fire piled on prepared ground? Why is it also piled on unprepared ground? For it is piled in the waters; and he who has not established the sacred fires is also in that world. He piles these bricks around it. [This applies] at the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Animal Sacrifice, and the Four-Monthly sacrifices. Moreover, they say: "[It applies] in all sacrificial rites. Indeed, the Śāṇḍilas used to say: "What kind of fire does one pile? One who piles the fire piles the *sattra* fire."

"By means of direct perception, [he builds] the year. Which fire does he build? "Building the Nāciketa fire, [he builds] the vital breaths by means of direct perception. Which fire does he build? "Building the Cāturhotriya fire, [he builds] the Brahman by means of direct perception. Which fire does he build? "Building the Vaiśvasṛja fire, [he builds] the body by means of direct perception. Which fire does he build? "Building the Upānuvākya-āśu fire, [he builds] these worlds by means of direct perception. Which fire does he build?

"Building this Āruṇaketuka fire-altar"—this refers to that very one which does not deviate from here nor from there. "Him"—thus [it is said]. He who knows the pairing of Agni becomes possessed of a mate. Water, indeed, is the pairing of Agni; he who knows thus becomes possessed of a mate.

"He knows"—he becomes the abode, he becomes possessed of an abode; "he knows, he knows"—he stands firm. At the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he builds that sun-like fire-altar reaching as high as the ankles. Building the swift fire-altar, he builds it facing the sun; he becomes possessed of a mate through the pairing. And one.

Flower, fire, wind, yonder sun, moon, stars, Parjanya, and the year—these abide as the sacrificial session (*sattra*). For a year, one should perform the *Sāvitra*, that *Nāciketa*, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the *Cāturhotriya*, the *Brahma Vaiśvasṛja*, the body, the *Upānuvākya*, the swift [fire], these worlds, this *Āruṇaketuka*—that which is yonder. Thus ends the twenty-second anuvāka of the first prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.22.

In the beginning, this world was indeed just water, a mere ocean. Prajāpati alone came into being upon a lotus leaf. Within his mind, desire arose: "May I create this. Therefore, what a person conceives with the mind, that he speaks with speech; that he performs with action. Regarding this, there is this verse: "Desire arose within him, which was the first seed of mind. Sages, searching in their hearts through wisdom, discovered the bond of being in non-being."

"Desire arose first within that [Being], which was the primal seed of mind. Sages, searching in their hearts with wisdom, discovered the bond of the existent within the non-existent. Thus it is said. Whatever desire one has, that comes to him who knows this. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, he shook his body. From its flesh, the rishis known as the Aruṇas, the Ketavas, and the Vātaraśanas arose. Those that were his nails became the Vaikhānasas; those that were his hair became the Vālakhilyas; and what was his vital essence became the waters.

Within [the waters] was a being in the form of a tortoise crawling about. He said to him: "Truly, you have become my skin and flesh. He replied: "No; I was already here before. That is the reason for the name *puruṣa*. He arose as the *puruṣa* with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. He said to him: "Truly, you were born first; you, therefore, perform this first. Taking water from here with his joined palms, he placed it in front.

"Truly so it is! Then the Sun rose; that is the eastern quarter. Then Āruṇaketu placed [the fire] on the south, saying, "Truly so it is, O Agni! Then indeed Agni rose; that is the southern quarter. Then Āruṇaketu placed [the fire] behind, saying, "Truly so it is, O Vāyu! Then indeed Vāyu rose; that is the western quarter. Then Āruṇaketu placed [the fire] on the north, saying, "Truly so it is, O Indra! Then indeed Indra rose; that is the northern quarter.

Then Āruṇaketu placed [the brick] in the middle with the words, "Even so, O Pūṣan. Thereupon Pūṣan arose; this is that direction. Then Āruṇaketu placed [the brick] above with the words, "Even so, O gods. Thereupon the gods, humans, ancestors, Gandharvas, and Apsarases arose; this is the upward direction. As for the drops that fell away, from them the Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas arose; therefore they were defeated, for they originated from the scattered drops.

Concerning this, there is this verse: "When the great waters came to the embryo, bearing Dakṣa and giving birth to the Self-existent (Svayaṃbhū), from that these creations were emitted; indeed, all this arose from the waters. Therefore, all this is the Self-existent Brahman. From that, all this became as if loose and as if unstable. Prajāpati indeed was that; having fashioned himself by means of his own self, he entered into that very thing. Concerning this, there is this verse.

"Having fashioned the worlds, having fashioned the beings, having fashioned all the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions, Prajāpati, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), entered into himself by means of his own self"—thus it is said. Having attained all this, having secured all this, he who knows thus enters into that very same [Prajāpati].
Thus ends the twenty-third Anuvāka in the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.23.

He takes four kinds of water. There are indeed four forms of water: the cloud, lightning, thunder, and rain. Verily, he secures these very things. He takes rainwater while it is shining [in the sun]. He places them in the east. These are indeed the waters that bestow spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Verily, he secures spiritual luster from the front. Therefore, one is more endowed with spiritual luster from the front. He takes well-water. He places them in the south. These are indeed the waters that possess brilliance (*tejas*).

He places *tejas* (brilliance) on his right side; therefore the right half is more brilliant. He takes the *sthāvarā* (immovable) [bricks]; he places them behind. The *sthāvarā* are indeed firmly established; thus he becomes established from behind. He takes the *vahantīḥ* (flowing) [bricks]; he places them on the north side. Indeed, these [bricks] are as if flowing, as if rising up, as if lowing, as if running with vigor (*ojas*). He thus bestows vigor upon his north side; therefore the left half is more vigorous.
He takes the *saṃbhāryā* bricks; he places them in the middle. "The *saṃbhāryā*s are indeed this [earth]," [he thinks]; "thus he finds support in this very [earth]."

He takes the *palvalyā* bricks; he places them on top. "The *palvalyā*s are indeed yonder sky; verily, he finds support in yonder sky," so it is said. He places them in the quarters; for the waters are in the quarters. The waters are indeed food; from the waters, food is born. Whatever food is born from the waters, that he secures. The seers Aruṇas, Ketavas, and Vātaraśanas built this very altar; therefore it is called the *Āruṇaketuka*. Regarding this, the following verse was spoken: "The Ketavas and the Aruṇas..."

"The seers girt with the wind, / For the hundredfold foundation, / Being concentrated, [attained] the thousandfold sustenance. Thus it is said. He who piles this fire and he who knows it thus finds a firm footing by the hundreds and by the thousands. [The sacrificer] takes the flowing waters, which are more radiant than Brahman-splendor; he places them above, as does the Āruṇaketuka, along with eight [others].
Thus ends the twenty-fourth Anuvāka in the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.24.

Having dug out the *uttaravedi* altar to the depth of the knees, he fills it with water, saying, "For the completeness of the waters. He lays down a lotus leaf (*puṣkaraparṇa*), a gold disk (*rukma*), and a human figure (*puruṣa*). The lotus leaf is indeed austerity; the gold disk is truth; the human figure is immortality. As much as there is, so much is this; whatever exists, that he thereby secures. He lays down a tortoise, saying, "He secures the very essence (*medha*) of the waters, and also for the attainment of the heavenly world. [He recites: "The waters, the waters, all the waters..."

"From here and from there, from yonder and from hence—Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya—may they together perform [this work] with wisdom. "The steeds are Vāyu; the lords are the rays," he says. "Fill the world, fill the gap; those which are the three highest-born ones," he says. "Indra’s roar, with the Vasus, indeed, for you," he says. He lays down five layers. Agni is fivefold (*pāṅkta*). As great as Agni is, him he builds up. With the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick he lays down the second layer. The Virāj consists of five feet; of that, this earth is one foot.

"The atmosphere is one foot; the sky is one foot; the quarters are one foot; that which is beyond the dust (parorajas) is one foot. He who piles this fire-altar, and he who knows it thus, stands firmly established in the Virāj itself. Thus [ends the section]; there is the verse "asti pṛṇa," the atmosphere is one foot, and six [syllables].
Thus ends the twenty-fifth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.25.1.25.

Having led forward the fire and kindled it, he places these bricks around it: at the Agnihotra, at the New and Full Moon sacrifices, at the Animal sacrifice, and at the Four-Monthly sacrifices. Now they say: "At all sacrificial rites. Then Āruṇi Svāyaṃbhuva said: "The entire fire belongs to Savitṛ; we consider this to be without further connection. Indeed, the powers of these [rites] are distinct. For what purpose does one pile the fire? One who piles the *sattra* fire. For what purpose does one pile the fire?

"One who piles the Sāvitra fire—what fire does he pile? One who piles the Nāciketa fire—what fire does he pile? One who piles the Cāturhotriya fire—what fire does he pile? One who piles the Vaiśvasṛja fire—what fire does he pile? One who piles the Upānuvākya or the Āśu fire—what fire does he pile? One who piles this Āruṇaketuka fire—what fire does he pile? Thus it is said. Agni is indeed a bull; one should not cause two bulls to clash, for his sacrifice would be destroyed.

Therefore, it should not be attached [to other rites]. One should pile the fire-altar in sacrifices that have the *uttaravedi* (high altar). For the fire is piled upon the *uttaravedi*. One desiring offspring should pile it; for this fire belongs to Prajāpati, and offspring belong to Prajāpati. He becomes possessed of offspring who knows thus. One desiring cattle should pile it; for water is the means of recognition for cattle. He piles the fire in the very place where cattle are recognized. He becomes possessed of cattle who knows thus. One desiring rain should pile it.

"Water is indeed rain; Parjanya becomes the showerer for him who knows thus. "One who is ill should pile [the fire-altar]. Water is indeed medicine; he provides medicine for himself. He reaches a full lifespan. "One practicing sorcery should pile [it]. Water is indeed a thunderbolt; he hurls the thunderbolt at his enemies. He lays them low. "One desiring brilliance, one desiring fame, one desiring spiritual luster, and one desiring heaven should pile it. Truly, there is only this much; as much as this exists, so much as there is, that much he obtains."

"I obtain that," he says. This is his vow: "While it rains, he shall not run; for water is immortality. It is for the non-interruption of immortality. He shall not void urine or excrement in water. He shall not spit. He shall not bathe naked. For this fire is secret; it is for the sake of not burning up this fire. He shall not step upon lotus leaves or gold. It is for the sake of not ascending over this fire. He shall not eat tortoise meat. Nor [should he eat] sweets that cause harm to the water; for they do not become sweets for the water.

"Water is free from evil. He who piles this fire-altar, and he who knows it thus. "He piles it, he piles it; one desiring offspring should pile it, he who knows thus. One should run toward water; one should eat. And four [verses]."
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section in the first chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.26.

"Whom indeed among these beings shall we establish? Indra and all the gods. "May Indra, together with the Ādityas, establish for us the sacrifice, the body, and progeny. "May Indra, accompanied by the Ādityas and the host of Maruts, be the protector of our bodies. "Float up! Float away! Become an egg; do not perish repeatedly. Release your own city, which begins in happiness and ends in suffering. These are the rays of the Self-born (Svāyaṃbhuva).

"Those who fashioned bodies—may they fashion your body. And may they not fail you in their manifestation. "Arise, do not sleep! Seek Agni, O Bhāratas! Satiated by King Soma, well-yoked with the sun at dawn! "A youth well-dressed... "The eight-wheeled, nine-gated city of the gods, Ayodhyā; within it is a golden treasury, the heavenly world enveloped in light. "Whoever indeed knows that [city] of Brahman..."

"The city enveloped in nectar; to him Brahmā and the Brahman gave life, fame, and progeny. "The radiant, golden city, completely surrounded by glory—the unconquered city—Brahmā entered. "Turning away one goes free from disease; turning away one goes free from wasting. He follows both here and hereafter, the wise man, among gods, asuras, and both. "Whatever a maiden utters softly, whatever a woman, whatever a devoted wife, and whatever is done that is unharmed [by ritual flaw]..."
"The fire follows after them," it is said. "Whether uncooked or cooked, whether sacrificers or non-sacrificers—those who go to heaven do not look back, provided they know Indra and Agni."

"Like grains of sand they come together, driven by rays from this world and that world; the seers with their spotted cows have given [the earth]," so it is said. "Depart, go away, and creep forth from here—those who are here, both ancient and recent; by days, waters, and nights, let Yama clearly grant him a dwelling place. "Let men hear, let the noble protect; those who are born of unploughed land and those born of ploughed land; those who are placed among maidens, among young girls, and among women who have lovers. "Those who have drunk the seed, those who have drunk the egg..."

"And those who have been offered as oblations upon the coals—both sons and grandsons—I, while young, [have sent] them to the realm of King Yama. "May there be for me a hundred autumns," thus [he says]. "That which is the Brahman, the support, of the Fathers and of Yama, of Varuṇa, of the Aśvins, of Agni, and of the Maruts who dwell in the sky. "May my fulfillment of desires be attained; for I am indeed that eternal one. Thus [he says]. "The firmament, the glory of Brahman, wealth, and riches; may the divine Waters and the Sons [of the Waters] be established here."
The city has nine gates, and Brahmā is the manifest; there are eight autumns.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh Anuvāka in the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.27.

"Viśīrṣṇī and Gṛdhraśīrṣṇī—drive away Destruction! Paribādha, Śvetakukṣa, Nijaṅgha, and Śabalodara—with this speech, drive them away together. O Agni, destroy their very sight! Envy, malice, hunger, wrath, and sorcery—they have established these; with a chariot like a *kiṃśuka* tree, O Agni, destroy their very sight! Thus ends the twenty-eighth anuvāka of the first prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.28.

"Sing forth to Parjanya, the bounteous son of Heaven; may he seek pasture for us. This speech is for Parjanya, the self-ruling one; may it dwell within his heart and bring him joy. May the wind be a source of delight to all people, and may the plants, protected by the gods, bear good fruit. Parjanya is the one who provides the embryo for the plants, for the cows, for the horses, and for women. Ten verses each for the ten-headed Parjanya.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth anuvāka of the first prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. "May power return to me; may life return, may fortune return; may spiritual knowledge (*brāhmaṇa*) return to me; may wealth return to me. "That seed of mine which today has fallen upon the earth, which has flowed into the plants, and which has entered the waters—this I take back again for long life and for splendor. "That seed of mine which is shed, that which is born from me again—with that make me immortal; with that make me possessed of good progeny."
And again, two.
Thus ends the thirtieth anuvāka in the first prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.30.

"From the waters, Tirodhā was born; there Vaiśravaṇa is ever present. Hide away our rivals—those whoever they may be who consume the waters. "The illusory power (*māyā*) of Tvaṣṭṛ, Vaiśravaṇa, [mounted] a chariot with a thousand seats, a thousand wheels, and a thousand horses. Having mounted it, come to us for our offering. "To whom all beings bring tribute—wealth, cattle, female elephants, and horses—may we abide in the favor of that worshipful one, bearing the splendor of Virāj, whose face is food."

"On Sudarśana and Krauñca, on Maināga and the great mountain, ending with the seven hundred *ṭṭāraga*s—this city of yours is to be withdrawn. These are the mantras. "The ritual procedure (*kalpa*) follows from hereon," it is said. If one should offer an oblation (*bali*), [he should say]: "This oblation is for Hiraṇyanābhi Vituda, the son of Kubera; obeisance to the Lord of all beings. Then, having offered the oblation, he should stand in worship: "Kṣattra, Kṣattra! Vaiśravaṇa! We are Brāhmaṇas."

"Salutations to you; do not harm me. Having entered into this, eat food"—thus [he says]. Then he should establish that fire in which he intends to perform this rite. "Tirodhā bhūḥ! Tirodhā bhuvaḥ! Tirodhā svaḥ! Tirodhā bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ! Sit in the sovereignty over all the worlds!"—thus [he says]. Then he kindles that fire in which he intends to perform this rite: "Tirodhā bhūḥ svāhā! Tirodhā bhuvaḥ svāhā!"

*Tirodhāḥ svāḥ svāhā! Tirodhā bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā!* At whatever time all his oblations have been offered—even those performed through the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa—at that time of the day he should employ [this mantra], even if it be after people have fallen asleep. One should not teach this to one who is negligent. All purposes are accomplished for him who knows thus. For one who does not know this, while hungry, all purposes are not accomplished. He who is a brother obstructive to you...

"He has taken refuge within my heart; therefore, I offer this first morsel to him. May he not frustrate my purposes; [I offer] *svāhā* unto me. "Homage we pay to Vaiśravaṇa, the king of kings, who overcomes by force. May he, the lord of desires (*kāmeśvara*), grant my desires to me, for I desire them. Homage to Kubera Vaiśravaṇa, the great king. The banners and the ruddy ones, the seers girt with wind—may they indeed establish a hundredfold support."

"May they, being concentrated, provide thousandfold nourishment. May the divine waters and plants be auspicious and most peaceful for us. O Sarasvatī, be very gracious; let not your expanse be visible [to me]. Thus [ends the section]. The horse, Bali, Bhūvas, Bhuvaḥ, Śrita, and the seven [constitute the group].
Thus ends the thirty-first anuvāka of the first prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.31

"One should observe this vow for one year, or for two months. This is the rule in brief. Within that, there are specific regulations: he should bathe at the three daily sessions; he should eat his meal at every fourth time-meal; or he should eat almsfood day after day. He should tend the sacred fire with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood while reciting the section beginning with "May my sensory power return to me. He should perform his necessary duties with water that has been drawn up and filtered. He should not accumulate possessions. [He offers oblations] to Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya.

The *vrata* oblations are offered to Brahmā Prajāpati, to the Moon, to the Nakṣatras, to the Seasons, to the Year, and to Varuṇa Āruṇi. The instruction is the same as for the *pravargya*. "The *aruṇa* sections and the seers"—thus they should study in the forest. Having murmured the two verses beginning with "Auspiciousness to our ears," and having touched water with the *mahānāmnī* verses, the teacher should give that [instruction] to him. With the verse "May they be auspicious to us, most peaceful," he touches the plants; with "O most merciful one," he touches the earth. The same applies at the conclusion. A cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

A copper vessel or a linen garment, or another white garment, or according to one's ability; thus, by the rule for Vedic study, he should recite in the forest. "The ascetic becomes meritorious, the ascetic becomes meritorious"—having recited this twice according to the rule for Vedic study, he should perform [the ritual].
Thus ends the thirty-second Anuvāka of the first Prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now follows the Peace (Śānti): May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones. With firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain the full span of life ordained by the Gods. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being.
Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace!
Thus ends the first Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 1.
Now begins the second chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
Hariḥ Oṃ! Homage to Brahman; homage be to Agni; homage to the Earth; homage to the plants. Homage to Speech; homage to the Lord of Speech; homage to Viṣṇu, the Great.
I perform.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.

"Oṃ! Indeed, the sacrifices of the gods and the asuras were both extended. 'We shall go to the heavenly world; we shall go! they [the gods] thought. Those asuras, having armed themselves, proceeded with violence alone. The gods, however, proceeded through celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and austerity (*tapas*). Those asuras became bewildered; they did not understand; they were defeated; they did not reach the heavenly world. By means of an extended sacrifice, the gods went to the heavenly world, and by means of a non-extended sacrifice, they brought about the defeat of the asuras. Thus it is said.

"The sacrifice of one who wears the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*) is indeed extended; that of one who does not wear it is unextended. Whatever a Brāhmaṇa who wears the sacrificial thread studies, he is truly sacrificing thereby. Therefore, wearing the sacrificial thread, one should study, officiate at sacrifices, or sacrifice oneself, for the extension of the sacrifice. Having draped the skin or the cloth over the right shoulder—raising the right arm and placing [the cord] under the left—it is the *yajñopavīta*. The reverse of this is the *prācīnāvīta*; the *saṃvīta* (wound around both shoulders) is for human rites. (1)

Thus ends the first anuvāka of the second prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 2.1. Indeed, the *rakṣas* demons were established in the *puronuvāka*. Prajāpati invited them with a boon; they chose this boon: "The Sun shall be our warrior. Prajāpati said to them, "Fight! Therefore, those *rakṣas* fight against the rising Sun until he has set. These *rakṣas* are indeed pacified by water consecrated with the *gāyatrī*.

"Indeed, those exponents of the Veda (brahmavādinaḥ), facing eastward at the twilight, scatter upward the waters consecrated with the Gāyatrī; these waters, having become thunderbolts (vajra), cast those Mandeha demons into the island of Aruṇa. By circumambulating to the right, they shake off evil. A learned Brāhmaṇa, meditating upon the rising and setting sun while performing [this rite], attains complete prosperity, for that sun is Brahman."
"Being Brahman itself, he attains Brahman—he who knows thus. Thus ends the second Anuvāka in the second Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇayajurveda. II.2.2.

"O Gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, O Adityas, release me from that; by the truth of Truth, protect me here. "O Gods, whatever untruth we have uttered with our speech out of a desire for life, release us from that here, O All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ), who are of one accord. "By Truth, O Heaven and Earth; by Truth, O Sarasvatī—protect us from the sin committed, whatever untruth we have uttered. "Indra and Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa, Soma, Dhātṛ, and Bṛhaspati..."

"May they release us from the sin that we have committed against others. "From the curse of one born of the same lineage, or from the curse of a kinsman, from the curse of an elder, or even from that of a younger; from whatever sin has been committed against the gods and remains unassailable—O Jātavedas, release us from that!"

"Whatever untruth we have committed with speech, with the mind, with the two arms, with the two thighs, with the two knees, or with the penis—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin, whatever evil deeds we have done. "With that [light] by which Trita emerged from the waters, by which Sūrya was released from darkness, and by which Indra abandoned all enemies—with that light, attaining light upon light, I have reached [the eye]. "Whatever debt remains unpaid by me here, by which I move about as a debtor to Yama—by this, O Agni, I become free from debt; even while living, I restore that to you."

"When my mother, made of that [substance], crushed me; when I transcend the atmosphere and the directions, O gods born in heaven; when I [transcend] the waters—this prayer I offer to you, O Varuṇa; you, O Agni, are our [protector]; you, O Agni, are our [protector]; you, O Agni, are the Unswerving (Ayās). Thus.
And deliver us from the sevenfold [bondage].
Thus ends the third anuvāka in the second prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Whatever debt I incurred while not gambling, or whatever I was unwilling to give back to people—I and Indra, acting in concert with Agni, shall release me from that. "What sins I have committed with my two hands, striking at the sound of the dice—Ugrampaśyā and Rāṣṭrabhṛt, those two Apsarases, shall wipe away those debts."

"O Ugrampaśyā, O Rāṣṭrabhṛt, whatever sins of gambling or unpaid debts there are—may he who is free from debt, being equal [to his obligations], not be bound by the cord of Yama in the world of Yama. "Release us from thy lower bond, release us from the highest; O Varuṇa, this prayer I offer to thee; O Agni, be thou our protector; O Agni, be thou our protector. "The Saṃkusuka, the Vikusuka, Nirṛti, and whatever whistling sound there is—drive disease far, far away from us, O ye sinless ones. "He has driven disease away, and the sorcery, and Nirṛti."

"By that [means], whoever seeks to harm us, him we drive away to him. "By the evil-speaker and the malicious-speaker, by the striker and the after-striker—by that [means], whoever else seeks to harm us, him we drive away to him. "We have united with splendor, with nourishment, with our bodies, with a gracious mind. May Tvaṣṭṛ here bestow wealth upon us; may he smooth over whatever in our bodies is injured. [This concludes] the *kṛtyā*, *nirṛti*, and the five [verses].
Thus ends the fourth section (anuvāka) in the second chapter (prapāṭhaka) of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Bestowing life upon you from every side, may this Agni, the most excellent, [grant it]. Your breath returns; I drive away your consumption. "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation, with ghee as your face and ghee as your womb, come! Having drunk the ghee and the sweet, pleasant milk of the cow, protect this child like a father protects his son. "O Agni, make him fit for long life and splendor; O Varuṇa, sharpen his keen vigor. O Aditi, grant him protection like a mother; O All-Gods, so that he may reach old age."

"O Agni, you purify our lives; bring us strength and nourishment. Drive misfortune far away. "O Agni, you who are skillful in action, purify yourself for us; bestowing upon me splendor, heroic power, wealth, and prosperity. "Agni is the seer, the purifying one, the priest of the five peoples; we seek him, the possessor of great wealth. "O Agni Jātavedas, drive away our enemies already born, and repel those yet unborn. Shine for us with a gracious mind, without anger; may we abide in your threefold protection, O Exalted One."

"Drive away our enemies who have already been born; O Jātavedas, drive back those yet unborn. Speak for us with a favorable mind; may we be victorious. Drive away our enemies. "O Agni, whatever person, like a wolf or a robber, seeks to harm us from all sides—slay them, O slayer of Vṛtra, and bring wealth to us. "O Agni, whoever seeks to injure us, whether he be a kinsman or a stranger—having made him our fuel, we consign him to you, O Agni."

"May Dawn and Night sweep away all the evil of him who curses us though we do not curse, and of him who curses us though we do curse. "O Gods, whatever rival or mortal enemy assails us, let nothing of him remain, as if of a log consumed by fire. "O Jātavedas, burn up all those who hate me and whom I hate, and those whom I hate and who hate me—burn them all together, O Agni."

"Whoever acts with enmity toward us, and whatever person hates us; whoever reviles us or seeks to harm us—crush them all to dust! O Brahman, sharpen my prayer; sharpen my vigor and my strength; sharpen my victorious sovereignty, I who am the domestic priest of this man. I have raised up their arms, and their splendor, and their strength; with my prayer I destroy the enemies and I exalt my own people."

"May mind come back to me; may life come back to me; may sight come back to me; may hearing come back to me; may breath come back to me; may intention come back to me; may thought come back to me; may devotion come back to me. May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable protector of my body, drive away all misfortunes. [This concludes] the section on nourishment, the office of the domestic priest, and four [additional verses].
Thus ends the fifth anuvāka in the second prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"We announce to Vaiśvānara that if our covenant with the gods has been deficient, may he, knowing this, release us from these bonds; may he deliver us from misfortune and reproach. "May Vaiśvānara purify us with his purifiers, for I hasten toward my hope and my covenant. Whatever sin I have committed here through ignorance or through the mind’s longing, I wash that away. "Those two auspicious stars in heaven named Vicṛtau (the Unloosers), may they extend life to us; this is the release of the bound."

"Desire to depart from the worlds; loosen the bonds so that you may release the bound one. Like an embryo released from the womb, follow all paths. "Knowing this, let the wise Prajāpati, the first-born of *ṛta*, accept [the gift]. May we follow the unbroken thread given by us beyond old age. Some follow the stretched thread, those for whom the ancestral inheritance has been bestowed.

"Let one give to the kinless; let him bestow gifts if he is able to give; for them, there is heaven. "Begin together, exert yourselves together; protect the common path with clarity (ghṛta). Whatever merit you have acquired or offered, whatever has been placed in the fire—for that sake, O husband and wife, exert yourselves here for the sake of the lineage. "Whatever we have harmed in the atmosphere, on earth, or in the sky, or whatever we have injured our mother or father—may Agni Gārhapatya lead us away from that sin; may he lead us out from the evils we have committed."

"The earth is our mother, Aditi our place of birth; the atmosphere is our brother, [warding off] the sin of imprecation. May the sky be our father; may you, O Father, be auspicious toward us. Do not seek to separate me from my kin in this world. "Where the benevolent doers of good deeds rejoice, having cast away disease from their own bodies—there in heaven, with unimpaired limbs and unbent, may we behold both father and son. "O Gods, whatever food I eat through falsehood, whether it be what I intended to give or what I did not give, or what I intended to do or did not do..."

"Whatever debt I have incurred toward the gods, whatever I have accepted as a gift—may Agni make me free from that debt. "Whatever food I eat in various forms, clothing, gold, cows, goats, and sheep—whatever debt I have incurred toward the gods, whatever I have accepted as a gift—may Agni make me free from that debt. "Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech—from all that, O Melit, deliver me; for you indeed know the truth as it is."
We two shall look after the son and the six.
Thus ends the sixth anuvāka in the second prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Indeed, there were seers who were naked ascetics with matted hair tied upwards; they lived as wanderers. Other seers sought them out; they moved about in concealment and entered into the *kūṣmāṇḍa* [plants]. The seers found them therein through faith and austerity. Those seers said to them, 'Why do you move about in concealment? They replied to the seers, 'Homage be to you, O Blessed Ones! By what means may we serve you in this abode? The seers said to them, 'Tell us a purifying prayer (*pavitra*) by which we may become free from sin. Thereupon, they [the *kūṣmāṇḍas*] beheld these hymns (*sūktas*)."

"Whatever offense against the gods we have committed, whatever debt I incurred while not gambling—bestowing life upon you from every side," with these [verses] they should offer clarified butter; "We announce it to Vaiśvānara," with this [verse] they should stand in worship; "whatever sin is prior to the killing of an embryo, from that you shall be released. Thus it is said. They offered with these [verses], and they became free from taint. One should offer with these at the beginning of rituals; purified, he attains the worlds of the gods.
Thus ends the seventh anuvāka in the second prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"One who considers himself as if unpurified should offer oblations with the *kūśmāṇḍa* formulas. "As a thief, as a slayer of an embryo, so does he become who sheds semen in a place that is not a womb. "He is released from whatever sin is prior to the murder of an embryo. "For as long as one undergoes initiation, being initiated, one offers these continuously. "One remains initiated for a year; by means of the year itself, one purifies oneself."

He who is consecrated for a month becomes purified from the year itself, for that which is a month is the year; he who is consecrated for twenty-four nights becomes purified from the year itself, for twenty-four half-months make a year; he who is consecrated for twelve nights becomes purified from the year itself, for twelve months make a year; he who is consecrated for six nights becomes purified from the year itself, for the year consists of the six seasons.

"He remains consecrated for three nights; the Gāyatrī has three feet; verily, by means of the Gāyatrī, he purifies his self. "He shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, he shall not sit on high [seats], and he shall loathe untruth. "Milk is the vow-food (*vrata*) for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for a Vaiśya. "Furthermore, one should prescribe this same vow even in the Soma sacrifice. "If he should think, 'I am becoming exhausted,' he should supplement his vow with boiled rice, parched grains, flour-meal, and ghee, so that there may be no exhaustion of himself."
Thus ends the eighth section in the second chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Verily, while the Pṛśnis were performing austerities, the self-existent Brahman flowed toward them; they became Ṛṣis, and that is the Ṛṣi-hood of the Ṛṣis. Desiring sacrifice, they approached that deity; they saw this Brahma-sacrifice, they took it up, and with it they sacrificed."

The Ṛg-verses which they studied became oblations of milk for the gods; the Yajus-formulas became oblations of clarified butter; the Sāman-chants became oblations of Soma; the Atharva-Aṅgiras verses became oblations of honey; and the Brāhmaṇas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Kalpas, Gāthās, and Nārāśaṃsīs became oblations of fat for the gods. By these they struck away hunger and evil; with their evil struck away, the gods went to the heavenly world, and the seers attained union with Brahman. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the ninth anuvāka in the second prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"These five great sacrifices are perpetually extended and perpetually completed: the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to Brahman. Thus it is said. When he offers even a single fuel-stick, that sacrifice to the gods is completed; when he offers water with the *svadhā* call to the ancestors, that sacrifice to the ancestors is completed.
