May I attain a full lifespan—may I attain a full lifespan! (35) O Lord of the Bay Steeds, increasing through these songs, fill up whatever is deficient in us here.

When you shatter the great enclosures for the sake of your praisers, may we then be those who receive the greatest portion. 36 We have uttered this prayer; may it not fail us. *Oṃ*! Peace! Peace! Peace! 37 May he establish [us] from afar; quicken those bound, so that they may see—seven [verses].
4.42 Prapāṭhaka 5: The Pravargya Brāhmaṇa.

Hari, Oṃ! May it be well with us; may it not forsake us. Oṃ! Peace, peace, peace! The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), desiring glory measured by success. They said, "Whatever glory shall first reach us, let that belong to all of us together. For them, Kurukṣetra was the altar. Of it, Khāṇḍava was the southern half, Tūrghna the northern half, Parīṇaj the hinder part, and the Marus the rubbish-heap. Glory reached the sacrifice of theirs, which was dedicated to Viṣṇu. It desired that [glory] for itself; by means of it, it departed. The gods followed after it.

Desiring glory, he pursued it; as he followed after it, a bow was born from his left side and arrows from his right. Therefore, the birth of the bow and arrows is auspicious, for their birth is from sacrifice. Though he was one, many could not overcome him; therefore, many who lack a bow and arrows cannot overcome a single man who possesses a bow and arrows. He smiled, thinking, "Though I am alone, many have not overcome me. As he smiled, his vital energy departed; the gods gathered it up in the plants.

They became *śyāmāka* grains; indeed, they are called *smayāka* for that reason, which is why *śyāmāka* is their name. Therefore, one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) should smile while covering his mouth, for the sake of maintaining his vital energy (*tejas*). He stood there, having strung his bow. Those *upadīkā* ants said, "Let us choose a boon: we shall subject this [earth] to you; wherever we dig, let us break through to water. Therefore, wherever the *upadīkā* ants dig, they break through to water, for they obtained this as their chosen boon.

He drew its bowstring. As his bow was being released, it struck off his head. That which rolled forth followed after heaven and earth; because it rolled forth (*prāvartata*), that is the *pravargya* nature of the *pravargya*. Because it fell with the sound "ghrām," that is the *gharma* nature of the *gharma*. "The power of the great one has fallen," they said; thus came the *mahāvīra* nature of the *mahāvīra*. Because they gathered it together from her, that is the *samrāj* nature of the *samrāj*. When he had been struck down, the deities divided him into three parts.

Agni belongs to the morning pressing; Indra to the midday pressing; and the Viśve Devas to the third pressing. Sacrificing with that headless sacrifice, they did not obtain blessings, nor did they win the world of heaven. Those gods said to the two Aśvins, "You two are indeed physicians; restore this head of the sacrifice. They replied, "Let us choose a boon: let a cup (graha) be drawn for us here as well. For them, they drew this cup belonging to the Aśvins.

Those two [Aśvins] restored this head of the sacrifice, which is the Pravargya. By means of that sacrifice possessed of a head, the sacrificers obtained the remaining boons and conquered the world of heaven. When one performs the Pravargya, he thereby restores the head of the sacrifice. By means of that sacrifice possessed of a head, the sacrificer obtains the remaining boons and conquers the worlds of heaven. Therefore, this Pravargya is like the chariot-steed of the Aśvins.
For these two [the Aśvins] dug up the *utkara* (mound of earth), and they spoke of the state of the Mahāvīra; they conquered seven.

He offers the oblation to Savitṛ for the sake of impulsion. He offers with [ghee] taken four times; cattle have four feet; verily he wins cattle. There are four quarters; verily he finds firm support in the quarters. The meters departed from the gods, saying, "We will not carry your portions of the oblation. For them, they set aside this [ghee] taken four times: for the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), for the offering verse (*yājyā*), for the deity, and for the *vaṣaṭ* call. In that he offers what is taken four times, he thereby gratifies the meters.

These, being pleased, carry his oblation to the gods. The exponents of the Veda say: "Should one offer [an oblation] in the house of the consecrated one, or should one not offer? The consecrated one is indeed the sacrificial food (*havis*). If he were to offer, he would cast the sacrificer—who has become the sacrificial food—into the fire. If he were not to offer, he would exclude the protector of the sacrifice. He should simply recite the *yajus* formula; thus he does not cast the sacrificer—who has become the sacrificial food—into the fire, nor does he exclude the protector of the sacrifice. Gāyatrī despised the meters.

The *vaṣaṭ*-call rushed toward her and cut off her head. Her essence split apart and fell away: one half entered the earth, and the other half entered the cattle. That which entered the earth became the *khadira* tree; that which entered the cattle became the goat. In that the wooden sword (*sphya*) is made of *khadira*, he restores the head of the sacrifice by means of the very essence of the meters. In that it is made of *udumbara* wood—the *udumbara* being strength—he restores the head of the sacrifice by means of strength itself. In that it is made of bamboo...

The bamboo is indeed brilliance; by means of brilliance he thus gathers together the head of the sacrifice. If it is made of *vikaṅkata* wood, he thereby wins light. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says as he takes up the spade, for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says, for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu*s among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint. This spade is indeed like a thunderbolt; "Thou art a spade, thou art a woman," he says for the sake of pacification. "O maker of the sacrifice for the gods," he says.

The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*. By saying, "To the gods, the performers of the sacrifice," he truly says this. He says, "Arise, O Brahmanaspati!"—with the *brahman* alone he approaches the head of the sacrifice. He says, "Let Brahmanaspati go forward!"—having gone forward, he approaches the head of the sacrifice. He says, "May Sūnṛtā go forth to the gods!"—the sacrifice is indeed Sūnṛtā. He says, "Toward the hero, the manly one, whose gifts are fivefold"—for the sacrifice is fivefold (*pāṅkta*). He says, "May the gods lead the sacrifice to us."

He makes the gods themselves the ones who lead the sacrifice. "O divine Heaven and Earth, may you two approve of me," he says; thus, with their approval, he brings together the head of the sacrifice. "May I succeed today in the head of Makha," he says. Makha is indeed the sacrifice; by this he means, "May I succeed today in the head of the sacrifice. "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee! he says; thus he carries it away after having specifically designated it. He carries it three times; these worlds are three.

From these very worlds he restores the head of the sacrifice. He carries the fourth part silently; thus he restores the head of the sacrifice from the unlimited. He first carries it from the clay-pit; therefore the clay-pit is most compassionate. "So much was there at first," he says; thus he restores the head of the sacrifice upon this very earth, so that there is no failure. Ants carry away that sap and essence of the earth which is the ant-hill; when the ant-hill serves as the supporting material for the head, it is for the sake of that strength and essence.

Verily, he wins the vigor and the essence of the earth; moreover, he wins the very sense of hearing, for the anthill is indeed the sense of hearing of the earth. He who knows this does not become deaf. Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra. Wherever he exerted his prowess, it did not hold firm. He exerted his prowess against a clump of *pūtīka* plants; there it held firm. He said, "Truly, you have given me aid (*ūti*). That is the reason for the name of the *ūtīka* plants. When they use *ūtīka* plants [in the ritual], it is because of this.

They place the oblation for the sake of the sacrifice itself. "Thou art born of Agni, O Prajāpati, the seed," he says; thus he secures that very essence which entered into the cattle. There are these five materials; the sacrifice is fivefold; as great as the sacrifice is, its head he thereby restores. If he were to collect the materials with the skin of domestic animals, he would afflict the domestic animals with pain. He collects them with a black antelope skin; thus he afflicts only the wild animals with pain.

Therefore, among animals being born, the wild animals are fewer. For they collect [the hair] from the fur while it is still moist with heat; for that part of his is fit for sacrifice (*medhya*). They go around [the fire] after enclosing it, to drive away the *rakṣases*. Many carry [the hair]; thus they bestow honor upon him. They place it on a dug-out spot, strewn with sand and enclosed, for the sake of peace. He pours warm water over it; he thereby bestows brilliance upon him. "May honey make thee sweet," he says.

By means of the *brahman* alone he bestows brilliance upon this [altar]. If he were to mix it with the potsherds of village vessels, he would subject village vessels to affliction. He mixes it with potsherds from a deserted site; for these are indeed not fit for use, and thus he subjects them alone to affliction. He mixes it with pebbles for the sake of stability, and also for the sake of peace. He mixes it with goat’s hair; for the goat is the dear body of Agni. With its own dear body he thus mixes it, and thereby with brilliance.

He mixes it with the hairs of the black antelope skin. The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; verily, by means of the sacrifice he mixes the sacrifice. He should not offer [it] as a *yājyā*. "The bamboo is unbroken for the sake of peace," he says. He carries it away; they smear it; it strides forth; it enters; it creates those being born for the sake of well-being. And eight.

He performs [the rite] in an enclosed space; this is for the securing of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). While performing it, he should not breathe toward it. If he were to breathe toward it while performing it, he would afflict his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with impurity. He breathes away from it; this is for the protection of the vital breaths. He should not allow the *pravargya* vessel and the sun to come between them. If he were to let them come between, he would become afflicted with skin disease; therefore, they must not be separated. This is for the protection of his own self. He performs it with a bamboo cane; the bamboo is indeed brilliance (*tejas*), and the *pravargya* is brilliance. Thus, by means of brilliance, he brings brilliance to fulfillment.

"Thou art the head of Makha," he says. Makha is indeed the sacrifice; this Pravargya is its head. Therefore he speaks thus. "Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice," he says, for these two are indeed the feet of the sacrifice; moreover, it is for the sake of stability. "I fashion thee with the Gāyatrī metre," he says; verily, he fashions it with the metres. He performs the *triyudh* (threefold striking); these worlds are three; it is for the attainment of these worlds. He fashions it with the metres; the metres are indeed vigor.

He makes it with vigor alone. He makes the hollow with a *yajus* formula for the sake of distinction. He makes it this large; it is commensurate with Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice. He makes it this large; it is commensurate with a joint of the sacrifice. He makes it this large; for such indeed is the vigor in a man—it is commensurate with vigor. He makes it of unlimited size for the attainment of the unlimited. He makes it neck-encircled for support. "Heat me with the heat of the sun," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself.

He fumigates it with horse-dung. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; [he does this] for the sake of having a common origin. "Thou art the footprint of the stallion, the horse," he says. Yonder sun is indeed the stallion, the horse; the meters are his footprint. Verily, by means of the meters, he fumigates it. "For the flame thee, for the radiance thee," he says; verily, he bestows brilliance upon it. The heated [pot] belongs to Varuṇa; he approaches it with one belonging to Mitra for the sake of pacification. "For success thee," he says; that is according to the sacrificial formula. "May the god Savitṛ lift thee up," he says.

Impelled by Savitṛ, he raises him up with the sacred word (brahman) and with the deities. "Not falling upon the earth, fill the quarters and the intermediate directions," he says; therefore Agni shines throughout all the directions. "Arise, become great, stand upright, you are firm," he says for the sake of stability. He who gazes at the Pravargya is liable to become blind. "I gaze at you with the eye of Sūrya," he says, for the protection of his sight.

"For the straight one, thee; for the good, thee; for the secure dwelling, thee; for prosperity, thee," he says. This [earth] indeed is the straight one; the intermediate space is the good; yonder [sky] is the secure dwelling; the quarters are prosperity. He thus prepares these very worlds for him. Moreover, it is for stability. "Here do I enclose so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with the people, with cattle, and with holy luster," he says. Verily, he encloses him with the people, with cattle, and with holy luster. For a Kṣatriya, he should say, "With the people"; verily, he encloses him with the people.

"With cattle," [he says]; this is for a Vaiśya. He encloses him with cattle indeed. He pours [milk] into the unanointed vessel, which belongs to the Asuras; he anoints it, making it belong to the gods. He anoints it with goat's milk. Goat's milk is indeed the highest milk; with the highest milk he thus anoints it. He does so with a *yajus* formula for the sake of distinction. He anoints it with the *chandasyas*; for by means of the *chandases* (metres) this [sacrifice] is performed; with the *chandases* he thus anoints the *chandases*. "Release the speech," he says.

Verily, he wins speech. "Cover it with strength," he says; verily, he wins strength. "Cover the oblation," he says; he has indeed made it an oblation. "O God, go before me; may I attain thee," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula. When one performs the Pravargya rite with the meters, it is endowed with vigor. "The meters have attained their perfection," he says; "the well-dwelling, uncrushed meters have been covered," he says—eight and...

"O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, praise the Gharma," he says. For at this time, the Brahman is indeed Bṛhaspati. Having addressed him, he proceeds, for his own safety. "For Yama thee, for Makha thee," he says. These are indeed its deities; with them he endows it. He sprinkles it with the boiling waters; he thus bestows brilliance upon it. He sprinkles it from the front; he thus bestows brilliance upon it from the front. He sprinkles it three times.

The sacrifice increases threefold; furthermore, it is for the sake of its purity. The Hotṛ recites [the invitatory verses]. This is for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas. He recites without pausing, for the continuity of the vital breaths. Although they are Triṣṭubhs, he recites them as if they were Gāyatrīs, for the vital breath is Gāyatra; thus he bestows the vital breath upon the sacrificer. He recites them continuously, for the continuity of the vital breaths and of the eating of food, and also for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas. If he were to recite a limited number, he would obtain only a limited result. He recites an unlimited number.

It is for the attainment of the immeasurable. The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice; Muñja grass is strength. In that the Veda is made of Muñja grass, he thereby provides the head of the sacrifice with strength. He offers the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); verily, he places the vital breaths within the sacrificer. He offers seven; there are indeed seven vital breaths in the head. Verily, he places the vital breaths within him. "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," he says; verily, he anoints him with splendor.

"Protect the earth from the heat," he says, as he throws down the gold; this is so that it may not burn through her. The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and Agni is all the deities. Having kindled the clippings (*pralava*), he throws them down; thus he restores the head of the sacrifice to the deities. Its tip remains uncrushed, for this is its sacrificial grass (*barhis*). "Thou art flame, thou art light," he says; he thereby bestows brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon him. "Sit down, for thou art great," he says; for he is indeed great.

The exponents of Brahman say: "These indeed are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Now, how is it that the Hotṛ priest does not pronounce blessings (*āśis*) for the sacrificer? Indeed, one sacrifice has its blessing at the beginning, while another has its blessing at the end. When he recites these sacrificial formulas (*yajus*), saying "Unassailable in front," the sacrificer secures the blessings from the very head of the sacrifice. He pronounces "long life" in the east, "progeny" in the south, "breath" in the west, and "hearing" in the north.

[He places] the *vidhṛti* on top. He thereby places the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) for him in a forward direction. Verily, he who arranges [the bricks] according to the quarters is liable to go mad after the quarters. "Thou art the horse of Manu, having many sons," with these words he touches this [earth]. This earth, indeed, is the horse of Manu, having many sons; he thus finds support in her very self, so that he does not go mad. "May she be easy of access to me; do not harm me," he says for the sake of non-injury. "Ye are piled, ye are piled around," he says; he thereby bestows honor upon him. This, indeed, is the head of the sacrifice.

As for the Pravargya: that Pravargya is indeed yonder sun; its rays are the Maruts. "Svāhā! Be encompassed by the Maruts," he says; he thus encircles yonder sun with its rays. Therefore, yonder sun is encompassed by its rays in that world; therefore, a king is encompassed by his subjects; therefore, a village headman is encompassed by his kinsmen. From the moment Agni was created, his luster reached the Vikaṅkata tree; therefore, the enclosing sticks are made of Vikaṅkata wood.

Verily, he wins light. There are twelve [bricks]; the year consists of twelve months; verily, he wins the year. "There is a thirteenth month," they say; in that there is a thirteenth enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), by that very means he wins the thirteenth month. "Thou art the intermediate space of the atmosphere," he says for the sake of distinction. "Protect the sky from the heat," he says, and places a piece of gold above; this is so that the sky may not be scorched.

Thus, by means of these two, he encloses him on both sides. "Worthy, you carry arrows and a bow," he says; he thus praises him. "You are the Gāyatra, you are the Triṣṭubh, you are the Jagatī," with these words he takes up the fans; he takes them up with the meters. "Honey, honey," he fans; honey is indeed breath; he thus bestows breath upon the sacrificer. They go around three times; for the breath is threefold. They go around three times.

The sacrifice increases threefold; furthermore, it is for the smiting away of the *rakṣases*. They go around three times again; thus six are completed. There are indeed six seasons; they find firm support in the seasons themselves. He who steps upon the dear body of the *gharma* indeed becomes one with a diseased skin. Truly, he who goes around a fourth time after having gone around three times steps upon his dear body. Indeed, Ugradeva Rājani stepped upon this [body] of his, and consequently he became one with a diseased skin.

Therefore, having gone around three times, he should not go around a fourth time, for the protection of himself. The fans are indeed the vital breaths; they shake them without interlacing, for the non-interlacing of the vital breaths and for their proper arrangement. Sitting down separately, they shake them; thus they find firm support in the quarters. They shake them upwards, for the attainment of the heavenly world. They shake them in every direction; therefore, this wind blows from every side. He recites as if placing [the offering]; this is the conclusion of the sacrifice.
"Others they establish as cool; the rays become the bow," he says, for the sacrifice has departed, for the sake of complete attainment; and two [verses].

"May Agni cause you to shine from the east with the Vasus and the Gāyatrī metre," he says. Verily, Agni causes him to shine from the east with the Vasus and the Gāyatrī metre. "May he, having shone, cause me to shine," he says; verily, he invokes this blessing. "May Indra cause you to shine from the south with the Rudras and the Triṣṭubh metre," he says. Verily, Indra causes him to shine from the south with the Rudras and the Triṣṭubh metre. "May he, having shone, cause me to shine," he says.

He utters this very blessing: "May Varuṇa cause thee to shine from the west with the Ādityas, by means of the Jagatī metre," he says. Verily, Varuṇa causes him to shine from the west with the Ādityas, by means of the Jagatī metre. "Shining, do thou cause me to shine," he says; he utters this very blessing. "May Dyutāna Māruta cause thee to shine from the north with the Maruts, by means of the Anuṣṭubh metre," he says. Verily, Dyutāna Māruta causes him to shine from the north with the Maruts, by means of the Anuṣṭubh metre.

"May he who has shone cause me to shine," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing. "May Bṛhaspati cause thee to shine from above with all the gods, with the Paṅkti metre," he says; thus Bṛhaspati causes him to shine from above with all the gods and with the Paṅkti metre. "May he who has shone cause me to shine," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing. "O divine Gharma, thou hast shone among the gods," he says, for he indeed has shone among the gods. "May I shine among men," he says.

"He indeed shines among men. "O Emperor, O Dharma, you have shone among the gods; may you be long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge," he says. For he has indeed shone among the gods and is long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge. "May I, having shone among men, become long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge," he says. He indeed becomes one who has shone among men, long-lived, radiant, and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge. "You are radiance; bestow radiance upon me; let there be radiance in me," he says. He thus invokes this very blessing.

If one were to say, "The *gharma* has been made radiant," without having caused it to become radiant by means of these *yajus* formulas, the *adhvaryu* would be without radiance and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) would be without radiance. But when, having caused it to become radiant by means of these *yajus* formulas, he says, "The *gharma* has been made radiant," the *adhvaryu* becomes radiant and the sacrificer becomes radiant. Afterwards, he causes it to become radiant with the *jagatī* metre, saying, "May I, being radiant, cause [thee] to become radiant.
He thereby invokes this very blessing. And eight...

The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice; the Upasads are the neck. He performs the Pravargya before the Upasads; thus he places the head of the sacrifice upon the neck itself. He performs it three times; these worlds are three; verily, from these worlds he wins the head of the sacrifice. They amount to six; the seasons are six; verily, from the seasons he wins the head of the sacrifice. He performs it twelve times; the year consists of twelve months.

From the year itself, he wins the head of the sacrifice. They amount to twenty-four; there are twenty-four half-months. From the half-months, he indeed wins the head of the sacrifice. Now, moreover, it should be anointed only once, for the head is one. He anoints it at the Agniṣṭoma; for as great as the sacrifice is, so great is the Agniṣṭoma. Of the sacrifice exactly as it is, he restores the head. He should not anoint it at the Ukthya; for the Ukthas are offspring and cattle.

If he were to draw [the Pravargya] at the Ukthya sacrifice, he would burn away his offspring and cattle. At the Viśvajit Sarvapṛṣṭha, he draws it; for the Pṛṣṭhas cause that which is unshakable to shake. By means of the Pṛṣṭhas, having caused that which is unshakable to shake for him, he wins it. "I have seen the Guardian," he says. The Guardian is indeed the breath (*prāṇa*). He thus distributes the breath among his offspring. "I have seen the Guardian," he says. Yonder sun is indeed the Guardian, for he protects these offspring. He thus makes him the protector of his offspring.

"He says, 'not sitting down,' for he does not sit down. He says, 'moving hither and thither along the paths,' for he indeed moves hither and thither along the paths. He says, 'clothing himself in those that meet and those that diverge,' for clothing himself in those that meet and those that diverge, he gazes upon all creatures. He says, 'he revolves within the worlds,' for he indeed revolves within the worlds. Here he says, 'Thou hast helped [the sacrifice] with honey for the two honey-drinkers, honey for the two honey-makers.'"

He prepares for him the two spring seasons. "Agni has come together with Agni," he says; he thus prepares for him the two summer seasons. "Agni has come together with Agni," he says, for this very Agni unites with Agni. "Svāhā! Agni has come together with fervor," he says; this has already been explained. He recites the subsequent verse: "Supporter of heaven, thou shinest through the mid-air and the earth," he says; he thus prepares for him the two rainy seasons. "For the heart thee, for the mind thee," he says.

"Śarad indeed prepares the two seasons for him," he says. "May you bestow the priestly offices (*hotrā*) among the gods in heaven," he says; by means of the priestly offices, he thus unites these worlds. "Lord of all beings," he says; this prepares the two winter seasons for him. "O divine Gharma, you who are heard by the gods, protect the gods," he says; this prepares the two dewy seasons for him. "Bestow upon us speech born of fervor (*tapas*), which is devoted to the gods," he says. That speech which is fit for sacrifice is indeed "born of fervor."

Verily, he wins that very [power]. "The germ of the gods," he says; for he is indeed the germ of the gods. "The father of thoughts," he says; for offspring are indeed thoughts, and of these the Pravargya is the father; therefore he speaks thus. "The lord of creatures," he says; for he is indeed the lord of creatures. "The thought of the seers," he says; for he is indeed the thought of the seers. "The god has united with the god Savitṛ, he has united with Sūrya, the radiant one," he says; he thus unites yonder Āditya and the Pravargya.

"O Gharma, you are the giver of life to us; you are the giver of splendor," he says. He thus invokes this very blessing. "You are our father; be mindful of us as a father," he says; he thus causes him to be mindful. There are nine of these openings; the tenth belongs to the wife. Indeed, there are nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, and the navel is the tenth. Verily, he places the vital breaths in the sacrificer. Moreover, the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is food; through the *virāj*, he wins the eating of food. The head of the sacrifice was cut off.

The gods restored it by means of the *hotrā*s (the priestly offices). The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) look upon it; for these indeed are the *hotrā*s. By means of the *hotrā*s alone he restores the head of the sacrifice. They look upon what is pleasing; for from what is pleasing Prajāpati created offspring—this is for the creation of offspring. They look upon what is pleasing; for from what is pleasing Parjanya rains; Parjanya becomes one who rains, and offspring flourish. They look upon what is pleasing; for what is pleasing is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

They become endowed with the splendor of Brahman (brahmavarcas). Those who study [the Veda] look [at the oblation]. They attain a full lifespan. The wife must not look [at it]. If the wife were to look, she would give birth; however, it would consume her offspring. If she were not to look, she would not give birth; yet it would not consume her offspring. Having screened [the oblation], he causes her to recite the *yajus* formula. She gives birth, and it does not consume her offspring. "May I move together with thee, rich in offspring," he says.

"For with a foot, offspring are indeed born. "The seasons are the head; he pushes forward [the cart] on all sides without it falling," he says; thus he prepares the autumnal seasons for him and secures them. "'Of the seers,' he says; he establishes the vital breaths.
'They come into being,' he causes [them] to recite; and there are four."

With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the cord for the sake of impulsion. He says, "With the arms of the Aśvins," for the Aśvins were indeed the two *adhvaryu* priests among the gods. He says, "With the hands of Pūṣan," for the sake of restraint. He says, "I take thee; thou art the girdle of Aditi," for the sake of making it a sacrificial formula (*yajus*). He says, "O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! These indeed are her divine names; he thus calls her by her divine names. He says, "So-and-so, come! So-and-so, come! So-and-so, come!"

These indeed are her human names; he calls her by means of her human names. They amount to six; for there are six seasons; he thus calls her by means of the seasons. "Thou art Aditi’s turban," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula. "Vāyu is thy calf," he says; for the calf has Vāyu as its deity. "May Pūṣan release thee," he says; for cattle have Pūṣan as their deity; he thus releases it by its own deity. "Cause it to be given to the Aśvins," he says.

The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; through them he provides medicine for him. "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible," he says; thus he praises her. "O Dawn, leave over the Gharma; O Dawn, protect the Gharma; leave over for the Gharma," he says; it is just as if one were to say, "Give this to so-and-so. "May Bṛhaspati attend upon thee," he says; Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods; verily, by means of the Brahman, he attends upon her. "Ye are the Dānavas, the Peravas," he says; verily, he makes them fit for sacrifice.

"He says, 'Enveloped on all sides by the red [blood],' for the sake of distinction. 'Overflow for the Aśvins; overflow for Sarasvatī; overflow for Pūṣan; overflow for Bṛhaspati,' he says; for it overflows indeed for these deities. 'Overflow for Indra; overflow for Indra,' he says; thus he provides Indra with his own portion. He says 'for Indra' twice; therefore Indra is the recipient of the greatest share among the deities."

"Thou art Gāyatra, thou art Traiṣṭubha, thou art Jāgata," with these words he takes up the hoof-receptacles; thus he takes them up by means of the meters. "Come hither with a portion of strength," he says; verily, he makes this a portion of strength for him. Indeed, when the Aśvins were restoring the head of the sacrifice, they said, "Let the *vaṣaṭ* be uttered first for us two alone. "O Indra and Aśvins, of the honeyed [juice] of the bees," he says; thus he utters the *vaṣaṭ* first for the Aśvins alone.

"Drink the Gharma, O Vasus; sacrifice, Vaṭ! he says. Thus he satisfies the Vasus with their own portion. If he were to utter *vaṣaṭ*, his *vaṣaṭ*-utterance would become exhausted. If he were not to utter *vaṣaṭ*, the Rakṣases would destroy the sacrifice. "Vaṭ! he says; thus he utters the *vaṣaṭ* in a hidden manner. His *vaṣaṭ*-utterance does not become exhausted.

"The Rākṣasas do not destroy the sacrifice; 'Svāhā! I offer thee for the rain-winning ray of Sūrya,' he says. That which is his auspicious ray is the rain-winner; it is for that very one that he offers him. 'Thou art honey, the oblation,' he says; verily, he makes it palatable. 'Heat the heat of Sūrya,' he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula (*yathāyajus*). 'I enclose thee with heaven and earth,' he says; verily, he encloses him with heaven and earth. 'With the intermediate space I support thee,' he says."

By means of the intermediate space, he thus brings it near. "Verily, no human being is worthy to support this," [he thinks]; therefore he says, "With the permission of the gods and the fathers, may I be able to support you. Thus, with the permission of the gods and the fathers, he takes it up. They indeed divide him in two when, having cast him out behind, they offer him in front. He says, "You are brilliance; follow after brilliance! Thus, he bestows brilliance upon him.

"Do not harm me who touches the sky; do not harm me who touches the intermediate region; do not harm me who touches the earth," he says for the sake of non-injury. "Thou art light; grant me light; grant me heaven; protect me from heaven," he says. He thus invokes this very blessing. The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and Vāyu is the self. Having raised it up, he recites the names of the winds; he thus restores the head to the self of the sacrifice. Without pausing [he recites], for the continuity of the vital breaths. He recites five times, for the sacrifice is fivefold.

As great as the sacrifice is, he restores its head. He says, "To Agni, accompanied by the Vasus, svāhā! Indeed, that sun is Agni accompanied by the Vasus; it is to him that he offers this. He says, "To Soma, accompanied by the Rudras, svāhā! Indeed, the moon is Soma accompanied by the Rudras; it is to him that he offers this. He says, "To Varuṇa, accompanied by the Ādityas, svāhā! Indeed, Varuṇa is in the waters, accompanied by the Ādityas; it is to him that he offers this. He says, "To Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the Viśve Devas, svāhā!"

Bṛhaspati is indeed the *brahman* among the gods; he offers him to the *brahman* itself. "To Savitṛ, the all-pervading, the far-reaching, the sovereign, the vigorous—*svāhā*! he says. Savitṛ is indeed the year, which is all-pervading, far-reaching, sovereign, and vigorous; it is to him that he offers him. "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Fathers—*svāhā*! he says. Yama is indeed the breath (*prāṇa*), who is accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Fathers; it is to him that he offers him. Thus he offers him to these very deities.

They amount to ten. The *virāj* consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* is food. By means of the *virāj*, he secures for himself the eating of food. By means of the two *rauhiṇa* offerings, the gods went to the heavenly world; that is why the *rauhiṇas* have their name. In that there are two *rauhiṇas*, the sacrificer thereby goes to the heavenly world by means of the two *rauhiṇas*. "May Day, with its banner, enjoy the light; may the fair-lighted one [enjoy] the lights, Svāhā! May Night, with its banner, enjoy the light; may the fair-lighted one [enjoy] the lights, Svāhā!"—thus he says.

He thus supports that very Āditya in yonder world from above by means of the day and from below by means of the night; therefore, that Āditya is supported in yonder world by day and night. "May the cattle sit down under the names of men," he says; "O Indra, come! he says; he divides, they strike, and he takes [the offering] for the sake of non-injury. "To the five-day [rite] accompanied by Āditya, svāhā! he says; "possessing a father," he says—these are four [syllables].

"May all the quarters sit upon the sacrificial fee," he says; thus he gratifies all the gods. Moreover, he protects him from a poorly performed sacrifice. "He has sacrificed to all the gods here," he says; thus he provides all the gods with their respective portions. "Drink of the honeyed gharma consecrated by Svāhā, O Aśvins," he says; thus he provides the two Aśvins with their portion. "Svāhā to Agni worthy of sacrifice, may there be well-being through the Yajus-formulas," he says; thus he causes him to flow toward himself.

"Then indeed he has offered the oblation: 'O Aśvins, drink the Gharma that gladdens the heart, with your daily aids! he says. Thus he provides the Aśvins with their share. 'May Heaven and Earth approve of you both,' he says for the sake of approval. 'Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Indra! Vaṭ to Indra! he says; for it is to Indra that the offering is first made. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, 'Recite the offering prayer for the Gharma. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering, for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasas. He recites the *anuyāja* for the sake of making the *svagā*."

"O Aśvins, you have drunk the Gharma," he says; this has already been declared previously. With the following verse, he praises it: "May Heaven and Earth approve of you both," he says for the sake of approval. "To him who is to be protected, according to his form; homage to Heaven, homage to Earth," he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). "Place this sacrifice in heaven, place this sacrifice in heaven," he says; he thus causes it to go to the heavenly world. "Go to heaven, go to the intermediate space, go to earth," he says.

He establishes him in these very worlds. "Go to the five regions," he says; he thus establishes him in the quarters. "Go to the gods who drink the *gharma*, go to the ancestors who drink the *gharma*," he says; he thus establishes him among both. When it overflows, Parjanya becomes rain-giving; therefore, that which overflows is auspicious. That which overflows toward the east belongs to the gods; that which [overflows] toward the south belongs to the ancestors; that which [overflows] toward the west belongs to humans; that which [overflows] toward the north—[belongs to the Rudras].

He causes it to swell toward the east and the north for the Rudras; he goes among the gods. Moreover, he causes it to swell in all directions; thus all the quarters prosper. He causes it to swell within the enclosing sticks so that its brilliance does not spill away. "Swell for food, swell for strength," he says; verily, he bestows food and strength upon the sacrificer. "Swell for the sacrificer," he says; verily, he invokes this blessing for the sacrificer. "Swell for my preeminence," he says; verily, he invokes this blessing for himself.

"For brilliance thee, for splendor thee, for power thee, for prosperity thee," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). "Thou art the Law (*dharma*), well-established in the Law; maintain the sacred formulations (*brahman*) within us," he says; thus he establishes him firmly in the sacred formulation itself. "If one should practice sorcery, [he should say]: 'May the wind not cause thee to spill! If he should hate someone, he should say: "I place thee in the breath of so-and-so; go to ruin along with so-and-so! With whomever he hates, with him he causes him to go to ruin.

"To Pūṣan, the showerer, svāhā! he says. To those very deities who have a share in the oblation, he offers it. "To the pressing-stones, svāhā! he says. To those very voices that are in the intermediate space, he offers it. "To the Pratiras, svāhā! he says. The gods who are the vital breaths are indeed the Pratiras; to them he offers it. "To Heaven and Earth, svāhā! he says. To Heaven and Earth he offers it. "To the Fathers who drink the Gharma, svāhā! he says. Those who are indeed performers of sacrifice—

Those ancestors are the drinkers of the *gharma*; it is to them that he offers this. 8. "To the Rudras, who are the *rudra-hotṛ*, svāhā! he says; thus he gratifies Rudra with his own portion. He anoints [the offering] on all sides; thus he propitiates Rudra from every side. He throws it out toward the north; for this is the quarter of Rudra; thus he propitiates Rudra in his own quarter. He touches water for the sake of purification. He does not look back; for if he were to look back, his eye would be subject to decay.

Therefore, one should not look [at the fire]. [The priest] says: "Carry me from day to night; protect me! This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; be kindled by it; grant me life; anoint me with splendor. He thereby bestows life and splendor upon him. [The priest] says: "Carry me from night to day; protect me! This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; be kindled by it; grant me life; anoint me with splendor. He thereby bestows life and splendor upon him. [The priest] says: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"

This is exactly according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Should the *agnihotra* be offered? Or should it not be offered? If one were to offer with a sacrificial formula, one would offer the oblations out of their proper sequence. If one were not to offer at all, Agni would be excluded. It should be offered simply with "Bhūḥ svāhā! Thus one offers the oblations in their proper sequence, and Agni is not excluded. He says, "The offering is sacrificed; honey is the offering. Verily, he makes it savory for him. He says, "Indra is his darkness in Agni. For Indra is indeed the breath, and Agni is the darkness.

He offers him, who is indeed the breath, into Agni as Indra. "Thou art our father; do not harm me," he says for the sake of non-injury. "May we partake of thee, O divine Gharma, rich in honey, rich in vigor, and rich in nourishment," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing. "Rich in *svadhā*, may we enjoy thee; do not harm me," he says for the sake of non-injury. Those who perform the *pravargya* rite are deprived of brilliance; they eat [the remains], and thus they place brilliance within themselves. For one year he should not eat meat, nor should he approach a woman.

One should not drink from an earthen vessel. O Rāma, one should not drink the remnants of his [food]; for that [act] diminishes his splendor (*tejas*). The gods and the Asuras were engaged in battle. As the gods were attaining victory, they deposited their sacred power (*brahman*) in the radiant sun, namely whatever is to be recited at dawn (*divākīrtya*). They protected it by means of this very vow. Therefore, this vow must be observed for the protection of one's splendor. For this reason, they say these sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) belong to Vibhrāj, the son of Sūrya.

"Svāhā! To you, for the rays of the sun," he says in the morning; "Svāhā! To you, for the stars," he says in the evening. These indeed are its deities; with them alone he causes it to prosper. "O unaging one, go forth to the quarters," he says. He causes it to swell within the enclosing-sticks of the ancestors. "Hold it steady," he says; to those drinkers of the *gharma* of speech, he offers it. "One should look after it while it is being offered," [the opponent asks]; "In the fire," he replies. They bestow it and protect it. Seven.

He offers three oblations with the verses, "O Gharma, that heat of thine which is in heaven... By means of the meters, he thus removes the heat from these worlds for him. First he offers one of this measure; then one of this measure; then one of this measure. These worlds are three; it is from these very worlds that he removes the heat for him. He says, "May Anumati favor us today," for the sake of Anumati. He says, "Thee for the highest protection of heaven"; verily, he supports these worlds from heaven. He says, "Thee for the highest protection of the Brahman"; verily, he supports offspring in these very worlds.

"By the protection of the breath for you," he says; thus he establishes the vital breaths within the offspring. The *pravargya* is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *pravargya* is truly that sun yonder. If one were to set it out facing south, west, or north, one would carry away the head of the sacrifice crookedly. He sets it out facing east; thus he restores the head of the sacrifice in front. He sets it out facing east; therefore, that sun rises in the east.

They bring after [the cart] the hoof-sockets, the winnowing-baskets, and the fire-sticks. Thus he makes him whole with his own self and whole with his body; he who knows thus becomes whole with his own self in yonder world. They are made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is indeed strength (*ūrj*); verily, he wins strength. For, having entered along the path, the Rakṣases seek to destroy the sacrifice. The Prastotṛ follows with the Sāman; the Sāman is indeed the slayer of Rakṣases; it is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. He approaches the finale (*nidhana*) three times; these worlds are three.

From these very worlds he drives away the *rakṣases*. Each person approaches the *nidhana* (concluding chant). For every person is possessed by a *rakṣas*; [this is] for the driving away of the *rakṣases*. If he were to set it down on the earth, he would afflict the earth with pain. If [he were to set it down] in the waters, he would afflict the waters with pain. If [he were to set it down] among the plants, he would afflict the plants with pain. If [he were to set it down] among the trees, he would afflict the trees with pain. Having placed gold [beneath], he sets it down.

Gold is indeed immortality; he thus establishes him in immortality. "Thou art auspicious, a bringer of well-being," saying this, he goes around sprinkling three times. For Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, he thus pacifies his heat. He goes around again three times; six [circumambulations] are completed. There are six seasons; by means of the seasons, he thus pacifies his heat. "The navel of Order has four corners," he says. This earth is indeed Order; the Pravargya is its very navel. Therefore he speaks thus.

"Thou art the seat, all-enlivening," he says; for this [altar] is indeed the seat. "Away with hatred, away with crookedness," he says, for the removal of the enemy. "O Gharma, this is thy food, this is thy soil-cover," with these words he fills it with curds mixed with honey. Curds are strength and the essence of food; verily, he endows it with strength and the essence of food. He who knows thus does not suffer from hunger. "Thou art Ranti by name, the celestial Gandharva," he says; he thereby declares his form, his greatness, his delight, and his kinship.

"Equal am I in life-span, equal in breath," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing. "May he perish who hates us and whom we hate," he says; this is indeed a spell of sorcery against him. "The tawny bull has bellowed," he says; for he is indeed a bull, a tawny bull. "Great like Mitra, beautiful to behold," he says; he thus praises him. "Thou art consciousness, thy womb is the ocean," he says; he thus causes him to go to his own womb. "Homage be to thee; do not harm me," he says for the sake of non-injury.

"O Soma, [I praise] Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva," he says. Whatever of this [Soma] they cause to fail while it is being prepared, that very thing he thereby causes to swell. "May Viśvāvasu sing this for us," he says—this has already been explained. With the following verse he sings over it: "May he, impelling our thoughts, protect our thoughts," he says; he thus arranges the seasons for him. "The Gandharva has proclaimed their immortals," he says. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the immortals; he thus arranges the vital breaths for him.

"O God, you who are the Gharma, go to the gods," he says; for being a god, he goes to the gods. "I here, a man, [go] to men," he says; for being a man, he goes to men. Indeed, when one is about to set aside the *pravargya*, he is liable [to lose] his offspring, his cattle, and his Soma-drinking. "Set aside [the vessel], O thou who art after my Soma-drinking! Go forth with me, together with offspring and with abundance of wealth," he says; thus he bestows upon himself offspring, cattle, and the Soma-drinking. "May the waters and plants be friendly to us," he says.

He utters this very blessing: "May those be ill-fated enemies who hate us and whom we hate"—this is indeed his act of sorcery. He who causes the *pravargya* vessel to be removed from the fire falls away from this world. Having returned, he offers oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire with two verses addressed to the Sun, beginning with "Upwards that" (*udu tyam*) and "The bright" (*citram*). The *gārhapatya* is indeed this world; thus he finds firm support in this very world. For yonder sun is indeed the heavenly world.

That which belongs to Sūrya—by that very [means] he does not depart from the heavenly worlds. "For the protection against the overstepping of Brahman," he says; he places [it], having excluded the Rākṣasas, for the sake of striking down the Rākṣasas. Indeed, gold drives away [evil]; "Let him praise," he says; "men," he says. Of this [gold], there are eight [verses].

The gods milked Prajāpati for his bright milk, but it did not suffice for them. Agni refined it, and it became the Śukriya Sāmans. From these, the essence that overflowed became the Śukriya Yajus formulas. These [formulas] are indeed the Śukriyas of the Śukriyas. Of these two, one is the milk of the Sāman, and the other is the milk of the gods. That which is the milk of the cow is the milk of the Sāman; that which is the milk of the goat is the milk of the gods.

Therefore, wherever they perform with these *yajus* formulas, they perform with milk. Thus they satisfy Prajāpati and the gods with milk and food. He indeed partakes directly of the *pravargya* for whom the *pravargya* is performed while he knows this. One should remove it onto the high altar (*uttaravedi*) for one who desires splendor; for the high altar is splendor and the *pravargya* is splendor—verily, by means of splendor he brings splendor to fulfillment. One should remove it onto the high altar for one who desires food.

The Pravargya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the Uttaravedi is the mouth. By means of the head, he unites with the mouth for the sake of eating food; he thus becomes an eater of food. Wherever they set this [Pravargya] aside, birds gather around it. Indeed, during that year, offspring gather around that place. Therefore, one should set it aside on the Uttaravedi itself, for the protection of offspring. One may set it aside either in front or behind. This light rises in the east, and it sets in the west.

He causes him to emerge from his own womb. He should cause it to emerge in the midst of the waters; for from the midst of the waters this light was born, and the Pravargya is light. Thus he establishes it in its own womb. If he should hate someone, he should cause it to emerge in the direction where that person is; for the Pravargya is Agni Vaiśvānara. By means of Agni Vaiśvānara, he thus sets him in motion. He should cause it to emerge upon an Udumbara branch; for the Udumbara is strength.

"Food is breath; heat is pain. "Here, by means of the pain of such-and-one, the son of such-and-one, I burn away his breath," he says. By means of pain itself, he burns away his breath; he swiftly meets with distress. Where the *darbha* grasses are spread out like a continuous line, there he should set down [the fire] for one who desires rain. These *darbha* grasses are indeed the waters called "unexhausting. Yonder sun, verily, sends forth rain from here; yonder sun himself bestows rain upon him.
Those waters flow restrained across the desert; the milk of the cow is the high altar; he establishes it; the cauldron flows.

Prajāpati was being gathered together; he was a sovereign (*samrāj*) when he had been gathered. He was the *gharma* when it was poured out; he was the *mahāvīra* when it was set down. This Pravargya is indeed that very sun. It assumed these names. Whoever knows this is known by his name. The exponents of the Veda say: "Whoever treats one who is more excellent according to his true name, he brings him prosperity; they bring prosperity to him who knows thus."

Therefore, knowing this, one should call it "the Gharma" by day and "the Saṃrāj" by night. These two indeed are his beloved bodies; these two are his beloved names. Verily, he endows him with his beloved body and his beloved name. His fame goes before him as he approaches the assembly. Gāyatrī departed from the gods; the gods regained her through the *pravargya* rite alone; they attained her through the *pravargya*. In that he performs the *pravargya* twenty-four times—

In that moment, he becomes the Gāyatrī; he attains the Gāyatrī. His fame spreads among his people from the very beginning. When it is poured out, it belongs to the Viśvedevas; when it is stirred, it belongs to the Vasus; when it is being scattered, it belongs to Soma; when the milk is being brought forward, it belongs to the Aśvins; when it is boiling, it belongs to the Maruts; when it has risen to the brim, it belongs to Pūṣan; when it is overflowing, it belongs to Sarasvatī; when it is taken up in the ladle, it belongs to Mitra; when it is being lifted up, it is brilliance; when it is being carried away, it is Prajāpati.

Being offered, he is indeed speech and clarified butter. This Pravargya is truly that sun; it assumed these names. He who knows this is known by his name. The exponents of the Veda say: "Since an offering does not consume what is made of clay, why then does this [Pravargya] consume it? One should reply: "This is Speech. Verily, one places speech in speech; therefore, it consumes it. This Pravargya is Prajāpati himself, distributed twelvefold. That which occurs prior to the *avakāśas* (the opening formulas)...

By means of that he created offspring. By means of the spaces he created the gods and the Asuras. That which was above the spaces, by means of that he created food. Food is Prajāpati; indeed, this [breath] is Prajāpati. They say: "When one is exhausted in his body, speech, when being offered, sustains what has been offered. This is he.

Becoming Savitṛ, he is chosen on the first day; by that, he goes to the desires. That he is chosen on the second day—becoming Agni, he goes to the gods. That he is chosen on the third day—becoming Vāyu, he goes to the vital breaths. That he is chosen on the fourth day—becoming Āditya, he goes to the rays. That he is chosen on the fifth day—becoming Candramas, he goes to the constellations. That he is chosen on the sixth day—becoming the Season, he goes to the year.

When he proceeds on the seventh day, having become Dhātṛ, he attains the Śakvarī. When he proceeds on the eighth day, having become Bṛhaspati, he attains the Gāyatrī. When he proceeds on the ninth day, having become Mitra, he attains the Trivṛt and these worlds. When he proceeds on the tenth day, having become Varuṇa, he attains the Virāj. When he proceeds on the eleventh day, having become Indra, he attains the Triṣṭubh. When he proceeds on the twelfth day, having become Soma, he attains the Sutyā.

Because it is kindled before the Upasads, therefore, from here, it goes toward those worlds beyond, burning. Because it is kindled after the Upasads, therefore, from those [worlds] beyond, it comes hither toward these worlds, burning. He who knows thus truly burns. 3. It goes to the Nakṣatras, it goes to the Virāj, it burns. "Peace be unto us! May that not forsake us!
Om! Peace! Peace! Peace!"
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Black Yajurveda.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Black Yajurveda:
"I sprinkle you with the Yajus-mantra for progeny, long life, and wealth."
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace, oṃ.

"Honor Yama, the King, the son of Vivasvat, the assembler of people, who has prepared a path for many along the great downward slopes—he who is the youth, whom others follow. "This garment has first come to you; depart from here, O man, leaving behind whatever you wore before. Look upon your sacrifices and charitable works, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given by you in various ways among your kinsmen. "I yoke these two carriers for you, to carry you to the world of the living."

By means of which two [paths] one may go to the abode of Yama and also to the world of the righteous. May Pūṣan, the wise one, the guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, drive you forth from here. He shall entrust you to these ancestors and to Agni, who belongs to the gods easy to find. May Pūṣan, who knows all these regions, lead us by the path most free from fear. Bestowing well-being, glowing, possessing all heroes, may he, the wise one, go before us without negligence.

May Āyus Viśvāyus protect you; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path ahead. Where the doers of good deeds sit, where they have gone—there may the god Savitṛ establish you. O Lord of the World, this is the oblation: *svāhā* to Agni Rayimant! O Sayāvarī of the man, we wipe away our sins so that no other shall come before us here until old age. O Sayāvarī of the man, I have not let your breath go astray.

With your body go to the earth; with your own offering go to the ancestors. Bring us offspring here. Do not grieve for me, O beloved goddess, since you, being virtuous, are going to the world of the fathers. O you who are desired by all, clothing yourself in the mist, turn back toward both our worlds with your moisture. This woman, choosing the world of her husband, lies down beside you, O mortal who have passed away. Protecting the entire ancient [tradition], bestow upon him offspring and wealth here.

Arise, O noble lady, toward the world of the living; come to this one whose life has departed who lies here. You have entered into this state of wifehood for your husband, the one who took your hand and wooed you. Taking the gold from the hand of the deceased—for the sake of prosperity, sacred power, splendor, and strength—remain right here, while we, being well-disposed, shall conquer all rivals and adversaries.

Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased for the sake of glory, for the warrior class, for vigor, and for strength—right here you are, and here we are, most gracious; may we conquer all rivals and adversaries. Taking the jewel from the hand of the deceased for the sake of glory, for the people, for prosperity, and for strength—right here you are, and here we are, most gracious; may we conquer all rivals and adversaries. O Agni, do not overturn this cup; it is dear to the gods and to those worthy of Soma. This is the cup from which the gods drink; in it, may the immortal gods rejoice.

Envelop yourself with the cow-hides as Agni’s armor; cover yourself completely with fat and marrow. Let not the bold one, exulting in his heat, seize you while seeking to consume you and cast you around. O Agni, do not burn him up, do not scorch him, do not strip away his skin or his body. When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas, then send him forth to the Fathers. When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas, then deliver him over to the Fathers.

When he goes toward this ill-guided path, then let him become subject to the will of the gods. Let your eye go to the sun, your breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to the cosmic law (*dharman*). Or go to the waters, if that is where it is beneficial for you; take your stand among the plants with your bodies. The goat is the portionless one—consume him with your heat! Let your flame consume him, let your radiance consume him! O Jātavedas, with those forms of yours which are auspicious, carry this man to the worlds of the doers of good deeds.

Truly, you are this; from this, you are that. Truly, you are his source. O Vaiśvānara, son, maker of the world, Jātavedas, carry him where the worlds of the doers of good deeds are. Knowing [the way], turn back toward us; may we conquer our adversaries with our bodies. (Four and [the preceding verse]).
Thus ends the first anuvāka in the sixth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 1 ||

"Obeisance to those who are the guardians of this path, svāhā! Obeisance to those who are the protectors of this path, svāhā! Obeisance to those who are the defenders of this path, svāhā! Obeisance to the one who makes it known, svāhā! Obeisance to the one who does not make it known, svāhā! Obeisance to the one who praises it, svāhā! Obeisance to the one who reviles it, svāhā! Obeisance to Agni, the performer of the rite, svāhā! Obeisance to him whom we do not know here, svāhā! Thus [he says].

"He who, perspiring, brings fuel, or heats his head out of devotion to you—protect him from every one who seeks to take away his wealth. "From this [earth] you were born; from you may he be born again. To Agni Vaiśvānara, for the sake of the heavenly world, Svāhā! These are the five verses following this.
Thus ends the second anuvāka in the sixth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Agni shines forth with his great banner; the Bull bellows aloud, making all things manifest. From even the ends of heaven he has reached down to me; the Mighty One has grown in the lap of the waters. "This is one light for you; beyond that is another for you. Unite with the third light. Being united, be beautiful to your own body, dear to the gods in the highest dwelling place."

"When they beheld thee with longing in their hearts as thou didst fly toward the firmament like a well-winged bird—thou of golden wings, the messenger of Varuṇa, the swift bird in the womb of Yama. "Run past the two Saramā’s sons, the four-eyed brindled dogs, by the straight path; then go unto the benevolent Fathers who rejoice in revelry together with Yama. "Those two dogs of thine, O Yama, the guardians, four-eyed, watchers of the path, lookers upon men..."

"O King, entrust him to those two; grant him well-being and freedom from disease. "The two broad-nosed ones, insatiable for life and possessing great strength, the messengers of Yama, wander among those who are powerless. May they give us back our life today so that we may behold the sun here once more, and may there be prosperity."

"Soma purifies itself for some; others worship with clarified butter. May he go even to those for whom honey flows forth. "Those who fight in battles, the heroes who abandon their bodies, or those who give away a thousand-fold sacrificial fees—may he go even to them. "Those who are invincible through austerity, those who have gone to heaven by means of austerity, and those who have performed great austerity—may he go even to them. "O rich ones, full of stones, take hold together! Arise, O friends, and cross over!"

"Here we leave behind those who were unfriendly; may we attain auspicious strengths. "That purifier of the god Savitṛ which is spread through the atmosphere in a thousand streams—by that with which he purified Indra so that he was free from affliction—I purify myself, my entire body. Those branches which fall away from the kingdom, being struck down while seeking a king—O Dhātṛ, may all of them, purified by this cleansing, unite us with progeny, wealth, and splendor."

"Beholding from above the darkness that higher light, we have gone to the god Sūrya among the gods, the highest light. May Dhātṛ purify [me], may Savitṛ purify [me], with the brilliance of Agni and the splendor of Sūrya. Bestow [this] upon me. (Eight [verses] follow.)
Thus ends the third anuvāka in the sixth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 3 ||

"The fire which we churned for you, as one would for a bull to cook [food], that very fire we now pacify with milk and with water. "That which you have completely burned, O Agni, that do you extinguish again. May the *kyāmbu* grow here, along with the *pāka*, the *dūrvā*, and the *vyalkaśā*. "O cool one, O you who possess coolness! O refreshing one, O you who possess refreshment! Bring this fire into union with the female frogs; pacify it! "Blessed be the waters from the desert for you; may the waters from the marshes be auspicious for you."

"May the waters of the ocean be auspicious for you; may the waters of the rain be auspicious for you. "May the flowing rivers be auspicious for your body; may the waters of the wells be auspicious for you. May the mist rain down auspiciously for you; may the dew settle upon you auspiciously. "Release him again, O Agni, to the fathers—he who, offered to you, moves by means of the *svadhā* offerings. Wearing a long life, let him approach his remainder; let him be united with his body, O Jātavedas. "Be united with the fathers, be united with the *svadhā* offerings, and be united with the merit of your sacrifices and good deeds in the highest heaven."

"Go where you choose for the earth; there may the god Savitṛ place you. "What the black bird has pecked at you, or the ant, the serpent, or even a wild beast—may Agni make all that free from debt, and Soma, who has entered into the Brāhmaṇa. "Arise, O body, gather yourself together! Do not abandon this limb, do not leave this frame! Go where you choose for the earth; there may the god Savitṛ place you."

"This is one for you, and another beyond that; enter into union with the third light. I shall praise you as one who grants rest; be beautiful and dear to the gods in the highest dwelling place. "Arise, go forth, run forward, and make yourself a home in the highest heaven! In agreement with Yama and Yamī, ascend this highest firmament. With the stones, with the wealthy ones, with that which is the purifier of the god Savitṛ, with those [waters] which have fallen from the kingdom—from the darkness, may Dhātṛ purify us."
"From this you were born; may he be born from you. To Agni Vaiśvānara, for the heavenly world, svāhā! Thus [the verse] ends with "let him settle in his dwelling," and there are five [verses].
Thus ends the fourth section in the sixth chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"May the god Yama come hither with his gracious aids, for he is indeed attached to these offerings presented here. May he sit upon the well-prepared sacrificial grass for my strength, for my progeny, and for the slaying of my enemies. When you two came, striving like twins, the god-seeking men brought you forward. Sit down in your own place, knowing it; be seated comfortably for our Soma-juice."

Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama. To Yama indeed goes the sacrifice, well-prepared, with Agni as its messenger. Offer the clarified-butter oblation to Yama and step forward; may he procure for us among the gods a long life that we may live it out. Offer the most honey-sweet oblation to King Yama. This homage is to the seers, the first-born, the ancient makers of the path. He who alone is the ruler of this world, of the earth, O Kauṣṭhya.

"Sing of Yama, whose fame is in the breaking [of obstacles], he who is the king that cannot be bypassed. "Sing of Yama, whose fame is in the breaking, he who is the king that cannot be bypassed; by whom the waters, the rivers, and the desert wastes were made firm, and by whom the sky and the earth were established. "King Yama presides over the gift of horses—those with golden girths, well-yoked, with golden eyes and iron hooves—that never fail. "Yama has supported the earth; Yama has supported this entire world. To Yama belongs everything that exists, whatever breathes, and whatever is protected by Vāyu."

"As the five, as the six, as the fifteen seers—whosoever should know Yama, let him speak, as does the one seer who truly understands. "With the *trikadruka* offerings he descends; the six wide [spaces] and this one great [space]. The *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and all the meters—these are all established in Yama. "Leading day after day cattle, horses, men, and the moving world, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is not satiated with the five classes of men. "In the realm of Vaivasvata, under King Yama, those people are separated."

"Those here who desire through truth and those who are speakers of untruth—O King, they are distinguished here, and then they come unto you. And those who bow to the gods and honor the Brahmins—in that tree with beautiful foliage where Yama drinks together with the gods, there our Father, the Lord of the People, remembers the ancients. Thus he remembers for those who know the makers of paths.
Thus ends the fifth anuvāka in the sixth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 5 ||

"I offer this oblation into Vaiśvānara; this is a thousandfold fountain with a hundred streams. In it, while it overflows, he bears the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather. "The drop has fallen upon the earth, upon the sky, upon this womb and that which was before. I offer the drop as it moves through the third womb, following the seven officiating priests. "This ocean, a hundred-streamed fountain, expanding in the midst of the world..."

"O Agni, do not harm Aditi, who yields clarified butter for the people, in the highest heaven. "Depart, go away, and creep apart from here—those who are ancient and those who are new. May Yama grant him a dwelling clearly distinguished by days, waters, and nights. "Savitar has placed these bodies in the lap of Mother Earth. Let them be joined with the inviolable [cows]. "Blessed be the draft-animals; blessed be the men; may the ploughshare plough happily."

"May the leather thongs be bound for prosperity; may you raise the goad for prosperity. O Śuna and Sīra, bestow prosperity upon us! "O Śuna and Sīra, with that milk which you created in heaven, sprinkle this [earth] here! "O Sītā, we revere you; be favorable to us, O fortunate one! So that you may be auspicious for us, so that you may bear good fruit for us! "O Savitṛ, I place these bodies in the lap of Mother Earth. With them, O Aditi, be a source of well-being!"

"Be released, O inviolable ones, paths of the gods; we have crossed over the furthest limit of darkness. We have attained the light, we have reached the sun, we have gone to heaven. "The winds blow forth, the lightnings fly down, the plants shoot up, and heaven overflows. Nourishment is born for every living being when Parjanya protects the earth with his seed. "Just as the five sons of Manu scattered the house-foundation for Yama, so do I scatter this house-foundation, so that we may be many in the world of the living."

"You are piled; you are piled around; you who are piled upwards, take your place! O Fathers, you are the deities. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity [may it be so]. "Swell up," "May your [milk] gather. Thus.
We have come to the inviolable ones, seven in number.
Thus ends the sixth Anuvāka in the sixth Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"I lift up the earth; placing this world around you, may I not be harmed. May the Fathers support this pillar for you; may Yama establish your dwelling here. "Approach this mother, the earth—vast-extending, very gracious, soft as wool, youthful, and full of bounty. May she protect you in her lap from destruction. "Rise up, O Earth; do not press down upon him. Be easy of access to him, easy of retreat."

"As a mother covers her son with her garment, so may the earth cover him. "Heaving yourself up, O Earth, you stand firm; let a thousand supports rest upon you. May these houses, dripping with honey, be his refuge here for all time. "May the female deer, the brown ones, the spotted ones, and the white ones be milch-cows for him; with sesame as their calves, may they yield nourishment for him, never failing, for all time. "This *svadhā* offering is placed for you in your dwelling, in your house, O Yama."

"Your name is Akṣiti (the Undying), so they say. "This sacred grass we offer to the ancestors; while living, may we offer what is higher to the gods. "As you ascend this, become worthy of sacrifice; in harmony with Yama and Yamī, may you go. "May the two trees not press upon you, nor you, Mother Earth. "For here you shall go to the Fathers, to find fuel in the realm of Yama. "May the two trees not oppress you, nor the great Mother Earth."

"Indeed, you shall go to Vaivasvata; you shall shine in the realm of Yama. "Mount this boat, Nala; follow the paths by means of Nala. "Having become the boat Nala, cross over, traverse, and go forth. Savitṛ has placed these bodies in the lap of the Mother Earth. "O Earth, be auspicious to them. "The Ṣaḍḍhotṛ [prays]: Let your eye go to the Sun, your breath to the Wind; go to Heaven and to Earth according to the Law (dharma)."

"Or go to the waters, if that is beneficial for you; take your stand among the plants with your bodies. "Go forth, O Death, along your own path, which is other than the path of the gods. To you who have eyes and hear, I say this: do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes. "Auspicious is the wind, and auspicious indeed is the sun's heat for you; may the plants be auspicious for you. May the quarters of the sky be favorable and gracious to me. "I set you in the world of the earth; you are the protection of such-and-such; the Fathers are the deity."

"May Prajāpati settle you with that deity. "I settle you on the back of the atmosphere, on the back of the sky, on the back of the quarters, on the back of the firmament, on the summit of the radiant one; you are the protection of such-and-such; the Pitṛs are the deity. May Prajāpati settle you with that deity."
And two [verses] beginning with "anapasphurantīḥ," addressed to the deity Uttara.
Thus ends the seventh Anuvāka in the sixth Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"May the sacrificial porridge, accompanied by cakes and clarified butter, sit here, upholding the earth and the sky above. Honor those who have prepared the womb and made the path, you who are here as the recipients of the clarified butter among the gods. This *svadhā* offering is placed for you in your dwelling, O Yama; this house is yours. Guard it, protect it—this which consists of ten syllables. I entrust it to you; may the Pitṛs and the deities not harm you therein. May Prajāpati settle you; through that deity [may it be so]."

"May the sacrificial porridge (caru), accompanied by cakes, boiled milk, fresh milk, curds, and honey, sit here, supporting the earth and the sky above. Honor those who have made the way, who have prepared the place; you who are here, possessing a share of the boiled milk, a share of the earth, a share of the curds, and a share of the honey. This is your seat; it is placed for you as *svadhā* in this house. It has a hundred syllables, a thousand syllables, ten thousand syllables, and imperishable syllables; protect it, guard it, I entrust it to you. In it, may the fathers and the deities not harm you. May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity [may you be established]. Thus.
He has ten cakes.
Thus ends the eighth Anuvāka in the sixth Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"I make these your imperishable *svadhā* offerings; those grains which I scatter here for you—may Yama, in agreement with the ancestors, make them into wish-fulfilling cows for you here. "The Brahmins know you to be the milk of the white plants; from their midst I take you, so that you may serve as a covering for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). "Bring a clump of *dūrvā* grass—this most beloved of mine—and let it grow most abundantly toward this direction, the quarter of men."

"Bring a bunch of *kāśa* grass for the warding off of demons; so that the malevolent ones who have perished from this quarter may never come back again. "Bring a bunch of *darbha* grass, the dear herb of the ancestors; may it take root along with its base, its stem, and its fruit. "Fill the space! These [bricks] yield milk for him. "Blessed be the wind, blessed be the sun's heat for you; may the herbs be auspicious for you. May all the quarters be favorable to you."

"May this indeed be some further relief for me from distress, which was thus performed by the Aśvins, Mitra, and Varuṇa. "May the divine Vanaspati ward off this [distress]—the Vanaspati from affliction, from destruction, and from hatred. "Thou art a separator; separate from us evils and hostilities. "O Śamī, pacify our evils and hostilities. "O Yava, keep away from us evils and hostilities."

"Go to the earth, go to the intermediate space, go to heaven, go to the quarters, go to the world of heaven; go to the world of heaven, go to the quarters, go to heaven, go to the intermediate space, go to the earth, or go to the waters, if that is beneficial for you; take your stand among the plants with your bodies. "The stony ones, the wealthy ones... "Whatever indeed is the purifier of the god Savitṛ... "Those which have fallen from the kingdom... "May we rise up from darkness... "May Dhātṛ purify us... "And may he purify the fruit."
Thus ends the ninth anuvāka of the sixth prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Ascending toward old age, chanting and striving in due order, may you live on. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the well-born and possessor of fine jewels, grant you long life that you may live. "Just as the days follow one after another, and as the seasons proceed in their ordained order, and as the later does not abandon the earlier—so, O Ordainer (Dhātṛ), arrange the lives of these people. "For no mortal has done harm to your body, O Agni. The monkey consumes the sharp point [of the arrow], just as a cow swallows its own afterbirth."

"May Agni, burning away our sin, purify wealth for us; may he, burning away our sin, [protect us] from death, Svāhā! We take hold of the ox for our well-being. May you, like Indra, be a carrier for us among the gods and a means of crossing over. "These living ones have turned back from the dead; may our invocation of the gods be auspicious today. We have gone forward for dancing and laughter, prolonging our life further. "When we go forth, effacing the footprint of Death, [we attain] a longer life."

"Bringing forth [strength] ever more abundantly, swelling with progeny and wealth, may you become pure, purified, and worthy of sacrifice. "I set up this boundary for the living; let it not pass beyond us to the further side. May they live a hundred long autumns; we ward off death with this mountain. "May these women, non-widows with noble husbands, anoint themselves with collyrium and clarified butter. Tearless, free from disease, and most auspicious, may these mothers first ascend to the place of origin."

"When the *añjana* from the three peaks was produced upon the Himavat, by that root of immortality we cause our enemies to perish. "As you, O herb, have burst forth from the earth, so may these [people] burst forth with renown, glory, and Vedic luster. "The goat is unborn; may it drive away from us sins and hostilities. "You are barley; barter away from us sins and hostilities."
Be a deliverer; we crush the three.
Thus ends the tenth Anuvāka in the sixth Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 10 ||

"May Agni burn away our sin; may he purify us with wealth. May he burn away our sin. "With a desire for good fields, a desire for a good path, and a desire for wealth, we sacrifice.
