May he burn away our sin. "Since the most excellent among these [the wise] have gone forward, and so have our patrons. May he burn away our sin. "Since the wise go forth on every side from the powerful Agni. May he burn away our sin. "O Agni, through those [patrons] of thine may we become wise; through thee may we become wise."

"May it burn away our sin," thus [he says]. "For you, O you whose face is everywhere, encompass all on every side; may it burn away our sin," thus [he says]. "O you whose face is everywhere, carry us across our enemies as if with a boat; may it burn away our sin," thus [he says]. "As one with a boat, carry us safely across like a river; may it burn away our sin," thus [he says]. "Like waters flowing down a slope, may sin flow away from us; may it burn away our sin," thus [he says].

"Like water from a well, may evil flow away from us; may our evil be burned away. "For bliss and for joy, I have returned to my own home; may our evil be burned away. "Indeed, neither cow, nor horse, nor man, nor beast perishes there, where this *brahman* is performed as a protective enclosure for the sake of life; may our evil be burned away."
Agha, magha, and four [others].
Thus ends the eleventh anuvāka of the sixth prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 11 ||

"We beheld a young woman approaching, a living one being led around for the dead. You who were shrouded by blind darkness—descending eastward and westward, do so for our safety. "When you, O Goddess, having been carried away by me while still alive, went to the world of the fathers; O you who possess all boons, clothing yourself in the sky, encompass both our worlds with your moisture. "May we sit near you with milk—you who abide in wealth, who are Agni, the honeyed wave, and the very essence of vigor."

"Be united with wealth, be united with splendor; attend to us for our well-being. "Those who are living and those who are dead, those who have been born and those who are yet to be born—to them I pour forth streams of honeyed ghee. "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality—I speak this forth to the discerning people: Do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi! "Let her drink water; let her eat grass. Om! Release her!"
And he killed two.
Thus ends the twelfth anuvāka in the sixth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Hariḥ Oṃ!
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 6.

Hariḥ Oṃ! May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutations to Brahman. Salutations to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the manifest Brahman. I shall speak of you, the manifest Brahman. I shall speak the Ṛta. I shall speak the Satya. May they protect me; may they protect the speaker. May they protect me; may they protect the speaker. Oṃ! Peace, peace, peace.
I shall speak the truth, and five [precepts].
Thus ends the first Anuvāka of the seventh Prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 1 ||

"Oṃ. We shall explain phonetics (*śīkṣā*). [It consists of: letter (*varṇa*), accent (*svara*), measure (*mātrā*), strength (*bala*), modulation (*sāman*), and continuity (*saṃtāna*). Thus has been stated the chapter on phonetics (*śīkṣādhyāya*). Phonetics is fivefold. Thus ends the second section (*anuvāka*) in the seventh chapter (*prapāṭhaka*) of the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* belonging to the Black Yajur Veda.

"May our fame be together; may our spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) be together. Now, therefore, we shall explain the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the *Saṃhitā* in five sections: concerning the worlds (*adhiloka*), concerning the luminaries (*adhijyautiṣa*), concerning knowledge (*adhividyā*), concerning progeny (*adhipraja*), and concerning the self (*adhyātma*). These they call the "Great *Saṃhitās*. Now, concerning the worlds: the earth is the prior form; the sky is the subsequent form; space is the junction; and the wind is the connection. This is concerning the worlds.

Now, with respect to the luminaries: fire is the prior form; the sun is the subsequent form; the waters are the junction; and lightning is the connection. This is "with respect to the luminaries. Now, with respect to knowledge: the teacher is the prior form; the pupil is the subsequent form; knowledge is the junction; and instruction is the connection. This is "with respect to knowledge. Now, with respect to progeny: the mother is the prior form; the father is the subsequent form; offspring is the junction; and procreation is the connection. This is "with respect to progeny."

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): the lower jaw is the prior form; the upper jaw is the subsequent form; speech is the junction; the tongue is the connection. This is with respect to the self. These, then, are the great conjunctions (*mahā-saṃhitā*). He who knows these great conjunctions as thus explained is joined with offspring, with cattle, with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), with the enjoyment of food, and with the heavenly world. "The teacher is the junction" refers to the world with respect to progeny.
Thus ends the third anuvāka in the seventh prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. ||3||

"He who is the bull of the meters, possessing all forms, who was born from the nectar of the meters—may that Indra strengthen me with wisdom. O God, may I be a bearer of the nectar of immortality. "May my body be observant; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my two ears. You are the treasury of the Veda, covered by wisdom. Protect what I have heard."

Bringing [prosperity], spreading it out, making for herself a long-lasting garment, clothing, cattle, food, and drink for me at all times—from that, bring me fortune, together with woolly livestock; *svāhā*. "May the students of sacred knowledge come to me, *svāhā*! May the students of sacred knowledge approach me, *svāhā*! May the students of sacred knowledge advance toward me, *svāhā*! May the students of sacred knowledge enter my house, *svāhā*! May the students of sacred knowledge find peace, *svāhā*! "May I be glorious among the people, *svāhā*!"

"May I be better than the worse-off; svāhā! May I enter you, O Bhaga; svāhā! May you, O Bhaga, enter me; svāhā! In you, who have a thousand branches, may I, O Bhaga, cleanse myself; svāhā! "Just as the waters flow down a slope, just as the months follow the decay of the day, so may the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacāriṇaḥ) come to me from every side, O Dhātṛ; svāhā! "You are a neighbor; shine upon me; come to me; svāhā! May the students of sacred knowledge, spreading out, bring peace; svāhā! May they come from every side, O Dhātṛ; svāhā! And one."
Thus ends the fourth anuvāka in the seventh prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"These three utterances (vyāhṛtis) are indeed *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvar*," [it is said]. Of these, Māhācamasya used to proclaim a fourth: "*mahaḥ*. That is Brahman; that is the Self (*ātman*); the other deities are its limbs. "Bhūḥ" is this world; "bhuvaḥ" is the intermediate space; "suvar" is yonder world; "mahaḥ" is the sun. Indeed, by the sun all the worlds are magnified (*mahīyante*). "Bhūḥ" is Agni; "bhuvaḥ" is Vāyu.

“*Suvar*” is the sun; “*maha*” is the moon. Indeed, by means of the moon all lights are magnified (*mahīyante*). “*Bhūḥ*” is the *ṛc*s; “*bhuvaḥ*” is the *sāmans*; “*suvar*” is the *yajus*s; “*maha*” is the Brahman. Indeed, by means of the Brahman all the Vedas are magnified. “*Bhūḥ*” is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*); “*bhuvaḥ*” is the in-breath (*apāna*); “*suvar*” is the diffused breath (*vyāna*); “*maha*” is food. Indeed, by means of food all the vital breaths are magnified. These, then, are those four [syllables] in their fourfold form.
"There are four sets of four utterances; he who knows them knows Brahman. All the gods bring him tribute. This world is the Yajus formulas, and it consists of two [verses].
Thus ends the fifth Anuvāka in the seventh Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"That which is this space within the heart—within it is this person consisting of mind, immortal and golden. "Between the two palates, that which hangs down like a nipple—that is the source of Indra. Where the hair-parting turns—having parted the two halves of the skull... "By *bhūḥ*, he establishes himself in fire; by *bhuvaḥ*, in wind; by *suvaḥ*, in the sun; by *mahaḥ*, in Brahman. He attains self-sovereignty; he attains the Lord of Mind. He becomes the Lord of Speech, the Lord of Sight."

He is the lord of the ear, the lord of consciousness. From this it follows: Brahman has space as its body; its self is truth; it delights in vital breath; its mind is bliss; it is enriched by peace and is immortal. Thus, O Prācīnayogya, do thou worship. And in the wind there is one immortal.
Thus ends the sixth anuvāka in the seventh prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Earth, the intermediate space, heaven, the quarters, and the intermediate quarters; fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars; water, herbs, trees, space, and the self—this is with respect to the objective world (*adhibhūta*). Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the in-breath (*apāna*), the upward-breath (*udāna*), and the equalizing breath (*samāna*); the eye, the ear, the mind, speech, and the skin; the skin, flesh, sinews, bone, and marrow. Having analyzed this, the Seer said: "All this is indeed fivefold (*pāṅkta*). By means of the fivefold, one attains the fivefold. Thus, all is one.
Thus ends the seventh Anuvāka in the seventh Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Om is Brahman," so it is said. "Om is all this," so it is said. Indeed, even when one causes [the announcement] to be heard or they cause it to be heard, it is by means of this imitation, "Om. They sing the *sāmans* with "Om. They recite the *śastras* with "Oṃ śom. The *adhvaryu* priest utters the response with "Om. The *brahman* priest gives his impulse with "Om. One consents to the *agnihotra* offering with "Om. A *brāhmaṇa*, about to speak, says, "Om"—thinking, "May I attain Brahman. He indeed attains Brahman. Om. Ten.
Thus ends the eighth Anuvāka in the seventh Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Righteousness and study and teaching; truth and study and teaching; austerity and study and teaching; self-restraint and study and teaching; tranquility and study and teaching; the sacred fires and study and teaching; the fire-sacrifice and study and teaching; guests and study and teaching; the human [duty] and study and teaching; and progeny and study and teaching.

"Procreation and the study and teaching of the Veda; procreation and the study and teaching of the Veda"—thus says Satyavacas Rāthītara. "Austerity," says Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi. "Only the study and teaching of the Veda," says Nāka Maudgalya, "for that indeed is austerity, for that indeed is austerity. Procreation and the study and teaching of the Veda—this makes six.
Thus ends the ninth anuvāka in the seventh prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"I am the shaker of the tree; my fame is like the ridge of a mountain. With the purifier held high, like a prize-winning steed, I am my own nectar—wealthful and resplendent, wise and sprinkled with immortality. Thus is the Vedic recitation of Triśaṅku. "I am six."
Thus ends the tenth anuvāka in the seventh prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

"Speak the truth. Practice righteousness. Do not neglect your private Vedic study. Having brought wealth that is pleasing to your teacher, do not let the thread of progeny be severed. One must not swerve from the truth. One must not swerve from righteousness. One must not swerve from what is beneficial. One must not swerve from prosperity. One must not swerve from private study and recitation. One must not swerve from the rites for the gods and the ancestors. Be one to whom the mother is a god. Be one to whom the father is a god."

"Be one for whom the teacher is a god; be one for whom the guest is a god. "Those actions which are blameless—those should be practiced, not others. "Those good deeds of ours—those should be emulated by you, not others. "Whatever Brahmins are superior to us, you must offer them a seat to relieve their fatigue. "One should give with faith; one should not give without faith. One should give with dignity; one should give with modesty; one should give with fear; one should give with a sense of shared responsibility."

Now, if you should have any doubt regarding ritual action (*karman*) or doubt regarding conduct (*vṛtta*), [you should act] as those Brahmins there who are reflective, disciplined, attentive, gentle, and lovers of dharma (*dharmakāma*) would act; so should you act there. And as for those who are accused: [you should act] as those Brahmins there who are reflective, disciplined, attentive, gentle, and lovers of dharma would act toward them; so should you act toward them. This is the instruction.

This is the instruction; this is the secret doctrine of the Veda; this is the command. It should be meditated upon in this way; indeed, it is to be meditated upon thus. You must not neglect the private recitation of the Vedas and the teaching of them; these you should meditate upon, and you should abide by these seven.
Thus ends the eleventh anuvāka of the seventh prapāṭhaka in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 11 ||

May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutation to Brahman! Salutation to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the directly perceived Brahman. To you alone, the directly perceived Brahman, have I spoken. I have spoken the *ṛta*; I have spoken the truth. May that protect me; may that protect the speaker. It has protected me; it has protected the speaker. *Oṃ*. Peace, peace, peace. "I have spoken the truth"—this is the fifth [chapter].
Thus ends the twelfth anuvāka in the seventh prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 12 ||

May there be peace for us through instruction; may there be peace for us both through that which is the source of the meters. He who is the earth, he who is "Om," and he who has recited the Veda as Truth—may there be peace for us; thus [there are] twelve. 12.

"May there be peace for us from the Great One"—this [verse] belongs to Āditya; the other twenty-three [verses] belong to the others. "May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Homage to Brahman! Homage to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak of the Ṛta; I shall speak of the Truth. May that protect me;
may that protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace."
Hariḥ Oṃ.
Thus ends the seventh Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 7.
Hariḥ Oṃ! May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we not harbor mutual hatred. Oṃ! Peace! Peace! Peace!

"Oṃ! The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Thus it is said. Regarding this, there is this verse: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. He who knows that which is hidden in the secret cave of the heart, in the highest heaven—he, together with the wise Brahman, enjoys all desires. From this very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; and from food, the person.
Now, this person indeed consists of the essence of food. Of him, this is the head; this is the right wing; this is the left wing; this is the trunk; this is the tail, the support.
Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the first Anuvāka in the eighth Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 1 ||

From food indeed are beings born, whatever dwell upon the earth; moreover, by food alone they live, and into it they finally pass away. For food is the eldest of all beings; therefore it is called the "all-herb" (*sarvauṣadha*). Verily, all food comes to those who worship food as Brahman. For food is the eldest of all beings; therefore—

"Food is called the universal medicine. From food beings are born; once born, they grow by means of food. It is eaten, and it eats beings; therefore it is called 'food' (anna). From this very one, which consists of the essence of food, there arises another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). By that [self], this [former] is filled. This one, indeed, is likewise of the form of a person. Following its human form, this [self] is of the form of a person. Of this [self], the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the head; the diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the right wing; the downward breath (*apāna*) is the left wing; space is the trunk; and the earth is the tail, the support.
And on this point, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the second anuvāka in the eighth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now begins the third section. The gods breathe along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*); so do humans and animals. For the vital breath is the life-span of all that is heard [in the Vedas]. Therefore, it is called "the whole life-span. Those who meditate upon the vital breath as Brahman attain their entire life-span; for the vital breath is the life-span of all beings. Therefore, it is called "the whole life-span. This is its very self within the body, which was the self of the former [sheath]. Therefore, distinct from this sheath consisting of the vital breath, there is another inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya*). By that, this [sheath] is filled.

Verily, this [Brahman] is indeed of the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). Following its form as a person, [the Veda] is of the form of a person. Of that [Veda], the *Yajus* is the head; the *Ṛk* is the right wing; the *Sāman* is the left wing; the *Ādeśa* is the body; and the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ* are the tail, the foundation. Regarding this, there is also this verse.
Thus ends the third section (*anuvāka*) in the eighth chapter (*prapāṭhaka*) of the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* of the Black Yajurveda.

Now begins the fourth section: "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—he who knows the bliss of Brahman, he never fears. This is indeed the embodied self of that [previous one], which was the self of the former. From this very one, consisting of mind, there is another inner self, consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). By that, this [former] is filled. He, indeed, is of the form of a person. Following his personhood, this [self] is of the form of a person. Faith is its head.
"Ṛta is the right wing; Satya is the left wing; Yoga is the body; and Mahas is the tail, the foundation.
Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the fourth anuvāka in the eighth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now begins the fifth section: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice; it also performs ritual acts. All the gods worship consciousness as the supreme Brahman. If one knows consciousness to be Brahman, and if one does not become negligent because of that, then, having cast off all evils from the body, one enjoys all desires. This is its very self within the body, which was the self of the preceding [sheath]. Therefore, different from this one consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). By that, this [self] is filled.

This very [Brahman] is indeed of the form of a person. Following its being of the form of a person, [the individual self] is of the form of a person. Of that [Brahman], joy (*priya*) is the head; delight (*moda*) is the right wing; rapture (*pramoda*) is the left wing; bliss (*ānanda*) is the body (*ātman*); and Brahman is the tail, the support.
Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the fifth anuvāka in the eighth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now begins the sixth section of the eighth chapter: "If one knows that Brahman is non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent. But if one knows that Brahman exists, then they know him to exist. This is his very self within the body, which is the same as that of the former [section]. Now, therefore, follow these further questions: "Does anyone who is ignorant go to that world after departing? Or does anyone who is wise attain that world after departing? He desired: "May I become many; may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity...

It created all this. Indeed, from food are born all creatures whatsoever that rest upon the earth; moreover, they live by food alone, and finally they merge back into it. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore, it is called the universal medicine (*sarvauṣadha*). Verily, all those who worship food as Brahman obtain all food. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore, it is called the universal medicine. From food beings are born; once born, they grow through food.

"It is eaten and it eats beings; therefore it is called 'food' (anna). From this very essence of the essence of food, there is another inner self consisting of breath (prāṇamaya). By that [self], this [former one] is filled. This one, indeed, is likewise of the form of a person (puruṣavidha). Following its form as a person, this [self] is of the form of a person. Of this [self], the out-breath (prāṇa) is the head; the diffused breath (vyāna) is the right wing; the down-breath (apāna) is the left wing; space is the trunk (ātman); and the earth is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the second anuvāka in the eighth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now begins the third section (Anuvāka). The gods breathe along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*); so do humans and animals. For the vital breath is the life-span (*āyus*) of living beings; therefore it is called "all-encompassing life" (*sarvāyuṣa*). All their life-span indeed goes to those who meditate upon the vital breath as Brahman. For the vital breath is the life-span of living beings; therefore it is called "all-encompassing life. This is its very self within the body (*śārīra ātmā*), which is the same as that of the preceding [sheath]. Therefore, distinct from this one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), there is another inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya*). By that, this [sheath] is filled.

Verily, this [Brahman] is indeed of the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). Following its person-form, [the Veda] is of the form of a person. Of that [Veda], the *Yajus* is the head; the *Ṛc* is the right wing; the *Sāman* is the left wing; the *Ādeśa* is the trunk; and the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ* are the tail, the foundation. Regarding this, there is also this verse.
Thus ends the third section (*anuvāka*) in the eighth chapter (*prapāṭhaka*) of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
Now begins the fourth section:

"From whence words turn back, together with the mind, failing to reach it—he who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing at any time. "Whatever there is here, having created that, he entered into it. Having entered into it, it became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*); the defined (*nirukta*) and the undefined (*anirukta*); the grounded (*nilayana*) and the groundless (*anilayana*); consciousness (*vijñāna*) and non-consciousness (*avijñāna*); truth (*satya*) and falsehood (*anṛta*). Whatever there is here, that became truth; they call it "Truth. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the sixth anuvāka in the eighth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now begins the seventh section: In the beginning, this universe was indeed non-existent (*asat*). From that, the existent (*sat*) was born. That made itself by itself. Therefore, it is called "well-made" (*sukṛta*). And what is this "well-made"? It is indeed essence (*rasa*). For only by attaining essence does one become blissful. For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss did not exist in the ether? He alone causes bliss. For when a person finds fearless support in that which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and without abode— ... [the text continues with the description of the Self]. ...he becomes free from fear. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7)

Then he becomes free from fear. For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Brahman], then fear arises for him. "In that very [Brahman] there is fear for the one who knows it but does not contemplate it.
On this point, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the seventh anuvāka in the eighth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

Now begins the eighth section: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear of Him the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni and Indra run, and Death as the fifth. This is an inquiry into bliss. A man should be young, a youth in his prime, a student of the Vedas, most swift, most firm, and most strong. Suppose this entire earth were filled with wealth for him; that is one measure of human bliss. A hundred times the bliss of humans is one measure of the bliss of the *manuṣya-gandharvas*.

"And for one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of the human *gandharvas* is equal to a single bliss of the divine *gandharvas*, and for one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of the divine *gandharvas* is equal to a single bliss of the ancestors who dwell in the long-lasting world (*ciraloka*), and for one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of the ancestors who dwell in the long-lasting world is equal to a single bliss of the gods born of their own nature (*ājāna*).

"And [the bliss] of one learned in the Vedas who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of those gods born of noble birth (*ājānajā*) is equal to one bliss of the gods by action (*karmadeva*), who reach the state of gods through their ritual acts; and [the bliss] of one learned in the Vedas who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of those gods by action is equal to one bliss of the gods; and [the bliss] of one learned in the Vedas who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of those gods...

"That which is the bliss of Indra is one hundredfold the bliss of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. "A hundredfold the blisses of Indra are equal to one bliss of Bṛhaspati, and of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. "A hundredfold the blisses of Bṛhaspati are equal to one bliss of Prajāpati, and of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. "A hundredfold the blisses of Prajāpati are equal to one bliss of Brahman, and of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire."

"That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun are one. He who knows this, having departed from this world, passes into this self consisting of food; he passes into this self consisting of vital breath; he passes into this self consisting of mind; he passes into this self consisting of consciousness; he passes into this self consisting of bliss. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
Thus ends the eighth Anuvāka in the eighth Prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 8 ||

Now begins the ninth section: "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—having known that bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing from anywhere. Indeed, this [knowledge] does not afflict him: "Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil? He who knows thus protects these two by means of the Self. For he who knows this protects both of these by means of the Self. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the ninth anuvāka in the eighth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. || 9 ||

The Knower of Brahman—this [section] consists of twenty-one parts: from the one consisting of the essence of food, there arise breath, the diffused breath (vyāna), the downward breath (apāna), space, and earth as the tail; this makes twenty-six. Breath, the Yajus, the Ṛk, the Sāman, the instruction, and the Atharva-Aṅgirasas as the tail; this makes twenty-two. That from which faith, truth, reality, yoga, and greatness proceed—this makes eighteen. Discernment, the dear, joy, delight, bliss, and Brahman as the tail; this makes twenty-two. Non-existence—this makes twenty-eight. Non-existence—this makes sixteen. "From fear of Him..."—this makes fifty-one. "From whatever source..."—this makes eleven. May He protect us both together. May He nourish us both together. May we work together with vigor.
May our study be radiant; may we never harbor mutual hatred.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Hariḥ Oṃ.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. 8.
